title: 景泰五年會試錄
text:
會試錄序
聖朝倣成周賓興賢能之典斟酌
隋唐以来進士明經之制三
歲一開科取士良法美意行
之愈久而益精以故得人之
盛超越隋唐而比隆成周焉
景泰五年春復當大比禮部
===
會試天下貢士前期臣濙臣
琦以考試官請
上命臣輅臣紹往蒞其事同考則
臣鼎臣齡臣潛臣溥臣諫臣
吉臣聰臣儼臣穆臣陬監試
則臣綱臣鵬及內外執事皆
遴選其人以充臣等受

會試錄序

聖朝倣成周賓興賢能之典，斟酌隋唐以来進士、明經之制，三歲一開科取士。良法美意，行之愈久而益精，以故得人之盛，超越隋唐而比隆成周焉。景泰五年春，復當大比，禮部會試天下貢士。前期，臣濙、臣琦以考試官請，上命臣輅、臣紹往蒞其事。同考則臣鼎、臣齡、臣潛、臣溥、臣諫、臣吉、臣聰、臣儼、臣穆、臣陬，監試則臣綱、臣鵬，及內外執事，皆遴選其人以充。臣等受
translation_en:
Preface to the Record of the Metropolitan Examination

Our Sacred Dynasty models itself on the canonical practice of the Accomplished Zhou in entertaining and promoting the worthy and capable, while adapting the systems of the metropolitan graduate (jinshi) and Classicist (mingjing) examinations from the Sui and Tang dynasties onward, opening the examinations once every three years to select scholars. The fine laws and admirable intentions behind this have grown ever more refined the longer they have been practiced; for this reason, the flourishing of talent obtained surpasses that of the Sui and Tang and rivals the height of the Accomplished Zhou. In the spring of the fifth year of the Jingtai reign (1454), it was once again time for the Great Triennial Examination, and the Ministry of Rites convened the Metropolitan Examination for the tribute scholars of the Empire. Prior to the date, Your Servants [Hu] Ying 胡濙 and [Yao] Qi 姚琦 petitioned for the appointment of Examiners, and His Majesty commanded Your Servants [Shang] Lu 商輅 and [Li] Shao 李紹 to go and preside over the affair. As for the Associate Examiners—Your Servants [Liu] Ding 劉鼎, [Yang] Ling 楊齡, [Lin] Qian 林潛, [Xu] Pu 徐溥, [Xie] Jian 謝諫, [Wang] Ji 王吉, [Lin] Cong 林聰, [Liu] Yan 劉儼, [Huang] Mu 黃穆, and [Wan] Zou 萬陬—and the Surveillance Officials of the Examination—Your Servants [Li] Gang 李綱 and [Zhang] Peng 張鵬—along with the inner and outer functionaries, all were carefully selected to fill their positions. title: 景泰五年會試錄
text:
命兢惕懼智慮弗逮有負
朝廷求賢之盛心誓殫公忠力
求報稱凡試士三千有奇取
文之中式者三百五十人遵
上命也臣惟成周取士先德行而
後文藝故當時濟濟多士實
皆吉人風俗之美治道之隆
===
可想見已隋唐以後始專尚
文辭雖曰文辭者德行之精
華然靡麗之習既滋而敦朴
之風寖失我
國家酌古準今罷詩賦之制以
經義論策試士必欲造理精
純立言簡切而弗戾於經於

translation_en:
… the command with reverent apprehension, fearing that our wisdom and deliberation might fall short and fail to live up to the court's magnanimous intention in seeking out the worthy. We vowed to exhaust our impartiality and loyalty, striving with all our might to reciprocate and fulfill our charge. In all, we examined more than three thousand candidates and selected three hundred and fifty whose essays met the standard, in compliance with His Majesty's command.

Your servant reflects that in the era of the accomplished Zhou dynasty, the selection of scholars put moral conduct first and literary and artistic skills second. Thus, the multitude of dignified scholars at that time were truly all virtuous men; the beauty of their customs and the flourishing of their governance can well be imagined. From the Sui and Tang dynasties onward, exclusive esteem began to be placed on literary composition. Although it is said that literary composition is the finest flowering of moral conduct, once the habit of extravagant embellishment proliferated, the custom of honest simplicity was gradually lost. Our Dynasty, weighing antiquity and taking measure of the present, abolished the system of testing by poetry and rhapsodies and instead examines scholars with expositions on the Classics, discourses, and policy essays, insisting that only those who attain a pure and refined grasp of principle, set forth their words with concise pertinence, and do not contravene the Classics or the…

title: 景泰五年會試錄
text:
道者始克中選科目取士崇
雅黜浮於斯備矣
皇上中興大業圖惟實才以資任
用於是申飭有司益嚴去取
杜僥倖而抑奔競一洗積習
之弊是以兹科得人之盛有
加於前諸士子際此
===
文明之運何其幸哉雖然諸士
子以科目進其造理固已精
純立言固已簡切於經於道
固已弗戾然所見者言耳行
將奉
大廷之對膺不次之擢其何以
副

punctuated: 道者，始克中選。科目取士，崇雅黜浮，於斯備矣。皇上中興大業，圖惟實才，以資任用。於是申飭有司，益嚴去取，杜僥倖而抑奔競，一洗積習之弊。是以兹科得人之盛，有加於前。諸士子際此文明之運，何其幸哉！雖然，諸士子以科目進，其造理固已精純，立言固已簡切，於經、於道固已弗戾，然所見者言耳。行將奉大廷之對，膺不次之擢，其何以副
translation_en: … the Way are able to pass the selection. Recruiting scholars through the examination categories, revering elegance and rejecting superficiality, has here reached perfection. His Majesty, in restoring the great enterprise, seeks out genuine talent to serve in official appointments. Accordingly, he repeatedly admonished the authorities to be ever stricter in acceptance and rejection, shutting off undeserved luck and curbing opportunistic competition, sweeping away at once the abuses of inveterate habit. For this reason, the flourishing abundance of capable men obtained in this examination surpasses that of previous ones. For all the scholars to encounter this era of cultural brilliance—how fortunate indeed! Even so, though the scholars advance through the examination categories—and though their grasp of principle is assuredly refined and pure, their words assuredly concise and incisive, and they assuredly do not run counter to the Classics or the Way—what has been seen so far is merely words. Soon they will respectfully answer in the Palace Examination in the Great Court and receive extraordinary promotions; how then will they live up to …

title: 景泰五年會試錄
text:
聖天子簡賢圖治之意亦惟踐其
言行其學以求弗背於初心
使德業有聞操履無玷隱然
以成周之士自處則庶乎科
目之光斯文之幸也故事登
名有錄錄成因序以勗之
嘉議大夫兵部左侍郎翰林
===
院學士兼左春坊大學士商輅
謹序

以成周之士自處則庶乎科
目之光斯文之幸也故事登
名有錄錄成因序以勗之
嘉議大夫兵部左侍郎翰林
===
院學士兼左春坊大學士商〔輅〕
謹序
punctuated:
聖天子簡賢圖治之意？亦惟踐其言、行其學，以求弗背於初心，使德業有聞、操履無玷，隱然以成周之士自處，則庶乎科目之光、斯文之幸也。故事登名有錄，錄成，因序以勗之。
嘉議大夫、兵部左侍郎、翰林院學士兼左春坊大學士商輅謹序。
translation_en:
…the Sacred Son of Heaven's intention in selecting the worthy and striving for good governance? It lies solely in fulfilling their words and practicing their learning, seeking not to betray their original aspirations, so that their moral character and achievements become renowned and their conduct and integrity remain unblemished, quietly conducting themselves as scholars of the flourishing Zhou era—then perhaps they will be a glory to the examination system and a blessing to our scholarly culture. By precedent, there is a record registering the names of the successful candidates; now that the record is complete, I write this preface to encourage them.

Respectfully prefaced by Shang Lu 商輅, Grand Master for Splendid Service, Left Vice Minister of War, Academician of the Hanlin Academy concurrently serving as Grand Academician of the Left Secretariat of the Heir Apparent.

translation_en:
Metropolitan Examination of the Fifth Year of the Jingtai Era (1454)

Administrators of the Tribute Examination (Zhi gongju guan)
Hu Ying 胡濙, Grandee of the First Class (Guanglu dafu), Junior Guardian (Shaofu), concurrently Grand Preceptor of the Heir Apparent (Taizi taishi), and Minister of Rites (Libu shangshu) [courtesy name Yuanjie 源潔, a native of Wujin County, Zhili; a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) of the gengchen year (1400)].
Sa Qi 薩琦, Grandee of the Sixteenth Class (Jiayi dafu), Right Vice Minister of Rites (Libu you shilang), and concurrently Vice Supervisor of the Household Administration of the Heir Apparent (Zhanshifu shao zhanshi) [courtesy name Tinggui 廷圭, a native of Min County, Fujian; a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) of the gengxu year (1430)].

Examiners (Kaoshi guan)
Shang Lu 商輅, Grandee of the Sixteenth Class (Jiayi dafu), Left Vice Minister of War (Bingbu zuo shilang), Chancellor of the Hanlin Academy (Hanlinyuan xueshi), and concurrently Grand Academician of the Left Secretariat of the Heir Apparent (Zuo chunfang daxueshi) [courtesy name Hongzai 弘載, a native of Chun'an County, Zhejiang; a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) of the yichou year (1445)].
Li Shao 李紹, Grandee of the Twenty-fifth Class (Fengxun dafu), Librarian of the Editorial Service (Sijingju xima), and concurrently Senior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy (Hanlinyuan xiuzhuan) [courtesy name Keshu 克述, a native of Anfu County, Jiangxi; a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) of the guichou year (1433)].

Associate Examiners (Tong kaoshi guan)
Yang Ding 楊鼎, Expositor-in-waiting of the Hanlin Academy (Hanlinyuan shijiang) and concurrently Companion of the Left Secretariat of the Heir Apparent (Zuo chunfang zuo zhongyun) [courtesy name Zongqi 宗器, a native of Xianning County, Shaanxi; a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) of the jiwei year (1439)].
Li Ling 李齡, Assistant Administrator of the Household Administration of the Heir Apparent (Zhanshifu fucheng) [courtesy name Jingling 景齡, a native of Chaoyang County, Guangdong; a tribute scholar (gongshi) of the jiyou year (1429)].
Ke Qian 柯潛, Companion of the Right Secretariat of the Heir Apparent (You chunfang you zhongyun) and concurrently Senior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy (Hanlinyuan xiuzhuan) [courtesy name Mengshi 孟時, a native of Putian County, Fujian; a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) of the xinwei year (1451)].
Qian Pu 錢溥, Admonisher of the Right Secretariat of the Heir Apparent (You chunfang you zanshan) and concurrently Examining Editor of the Hanlin Academy (Hanlinyuan jiantao) [courtesy name Yuanpu 原溥, a native of Huating County, Zhili; a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) of the jiwei year (1439)].
Huang Jian 黃諫, Junior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy (Hanlinyuan bianxiu) and Gentleman for Literature (Wenlin lang) [courtesy name Tingchen 廷臣, a native of Lan County, Shaanxi; a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) of the renxu year (1442)].
Liu Ji 劉吉, Junior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy (Hanlinyuan bianxiu) and Gentleman for Literature (Wenlin lang) [courtesy name Youzhi 祐之, a native of Boye County, Zhili; a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) of the wuchen year (1448)].
Lin Cong 林聰, Chief Supervising Secretary of the Office of Scrutiny for Personnel (Like du jishizhong) [courtesy name Jicong 季聰, a native of Ningde County, Fujian; a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) of the jiwei year (1439)].

title: 景泰五年會試錄
text:
第壹場
四書
子在川上曰逝者如斯夫不舍晝夜
忠恕違道不遠施諸己而不願亦勿施於
人
請野九一而助國中什一使自賦卿以下
必有圭田圭田五十畝餘夫二十五
畝
易
===
君子以成德為行日可見之行也
九五觀我生君子无咎象曰觀我生觀民
也
卦有小大辭有險易辭也者各指其所之
黃帝堯舜氏作通其變使民不倦神而化
之使民宜之易窮則變變則通通則
久是以自天祐之吉无不利黃帝堯

First Session

Four Books (Sishu):
The Master, standing by a stream, said: "Everything passes on just like this, not ceasing day or night!"
Conscientiousness and reciprocity are not far from the Way. What you do not wish done to yourself, do not do to others.
I would ask that in the countryside the nine-squares system be used to provide mutual aid, and in the capital area a tenth be levied to let the people pay their own taxes. From the Ministers down, all must have ritual land (guitian), the ritual land consisting of fifty mu; extra adult males shall receive twenty-five mu.

Book of Changes (Yi):
The superior man takes perfected virtue as his conduct—conduct that can be seen every day.
Nine in the fifth place: Contemplating my own life; for the superior man, there is no blame. The Commentary on the Images (Xiang) says: "'Contemplating my own life' means contemplating the condition of the people."
Among the hexagrams there are small and great, and among the appended statements there are expressions of danger and ease. Each statement points to where the tendency is going.
When the clans of the Yellow Emperor (Huangdi), Yao, and Shun arose, they carried through the changes so that the people did not grow weary; they transformed things with a wondrous spirit so that the people found them fitting. In the Changes, when a state reaches its limit, it alters; by altering, it achieves continuity; by achieving continuity, it endures. Therefore, "help comes to him from Heaven; there is good fortune and nothing that is not beneficial." The Yellow Emperor, Yao, and Shun let their upper and lower garments hang down and the world was well governed; they probably took this idea from the hexagrams Qian and Kun.

translation_en:
“[When I] go against [what is right], you should correct me. You must not comply to my face, and after retiring hold back-talk. Be reverent, O my four neighbors!”
“The Jiang and the Han pay court to the sea; the Nine Rivers are brought into great order; the Tuo and the Qian have been guided into their channels; the land of Yun appears, and Meng is made cultivable.”
“Reverently honor the Way of Heaven, and forever preserve the Mandate of Heaven.”
“Yu then succeeded and rose up, and Heaven thereupon bestowed on Yu the Great Plan in nine divisions, whereby the invariable human relations were set in order. The first is called the Five Elements; the second is called the reverent practice of the Five Demeanors; the third is called the earnest devotion to the Eight Modes of Government; the fourth is called the harmonious use of the Five Regulators of Time; the fifth is called the establishment and practice of the Royal Perfection; the sixth is called the governing use of the Three Virtues; the seventh is called the intelligent use of the Examination of Doubts; the eighth is called the thoughtful use of the Various Verifications; the ninth is called the encouraging use of the Five Blessings, and the awe-inspiring use of the Six Extremities.”
[Note: The classic heading “Book of Odes (詩)” is omitted in the transcription here.]
“My four stallions are very large and strong, and the six reins are in the hand. The piebald and the black-mouthed bay are in the inside; the yellow-and-black and the pure black are the outside horses. Put together are the dragon-figured shields, and gilt are the buckles for the inner reins. I think of my lord, how gentle he is in the town! What time can be fixed for his return? Why am I thus longing for him!”
“Do not follow and humor them, so as not to make them greatly negligent. What ought not to be said, do not say; what proceeds from no good ground, do not utter. From tipsy words, make them bring out a hornless ram. With three cups they lose their memory—how much less dare they drink more again!”
“God made a state and made a match for it, from Taibo and Wang Ji.”

translation_en:
… the Viscount of Chen, the Viscount of Ju, the Viscount of Zhu, and a representative of Qin at Wen. The Heavenly King hunted at Heyang. The Duke had an audience at the King's temporary residence. The feudal lords thereupon besieged Xu. The Duke arrived back from besieging Xu. (28th year of Duke Xi)
In spring, in the King's first month, the Duke went to Qi. In summer, Zhongsun Mie went to the capital. (9th year of Duke Xuan) On the bingwu day, a covenant was made with Xun Geng. On the dingwei day, a covenant was made with Sun Liangfu. (3rd year of Duke Cheng)

Record of Rites (Liji)
The gui and zhang jade tablets are presented alone; the hu and huang jades are presented along with goblets. In sacrifices to ghosts and spirits, a single mat is used. When the feudal lords hold court, the Great Officers are greeted individually, and the Service-men are greeted as a group.
Whenever attending upon a ruler, one's sash hangs down, one's feet seem to tread upon the hem of the lower garment, one's chin is inclined like the eaves of a roof, and one's hands hang clasped together; one looks downward and listens upward, one's gaze ranging from the girdle to the collar, and in listening one turns toward the left.
The gentleman regards this as showing respect; only after that does he teach the common people with what he is capable of, not neglecting their appointed times and proper measures. When there is an accomplished achievement, only then does he prepare the carvings, engravings, patterns, and embroidered emblems in order to carry it on.
When sageliness is established and is carried forward with reverence, it is called ritual propriety (li); when ritual propriety gives embodiment to the distinction between elder and younger, it is called virtue (de). Virtue means obtaining it within one's own person. Therefore it is said: Those in antiquity who studied the arts and the Way did so in order to obtain it in their own persons.

punctuated: 之言，而卒成其書者，曾子門人、子思之徒也。及子思作《中庸》，乃有與《論語》異者。《論語》曰「子罕言命與仁」，「性與天道不可得聞」，而《中庸》首言「天命謂性」，曰「仁者人也」、「誠者天道」，何歟？《論語》答子路問事鬼神曰「未能事人，焉能事鬼」，而《中庸》極言鬼神之德，「使天下之人齊明盛服以承祭祀」，又何歟？《論語》曰「殷禮吾能言之，宋不足徵也」、「如用之，則吾從先進」，《中庸》曰「吾學殷禮，有宋存焉；吾學周禮，今用□，吾從周」，何言之戾歟？《論語》曰「三分天下有其二，以服事殷，周之德，可謂至德也已矣」，《中庸》曰「武王其達孝矣乎！善繼人之志，善述人之事」，夫以文王終身事紂，而武王不崇朝而伐之，謂之善繼志述事，何歟？《論語》於夫子稱「子」，而《中庸》乃稱「仲尼」，豈孫可以字其祖歟？是皆不能無疑者。先儒謂《中庸》乃孔門傳授心法，何…
translation_en: …words, and those who finally completed the book were the disciples of Zengzi 曾子 and the followers of Zisi 子思. Yet when Zisi composed the Doctrine of the Mean (Zhongyong 中庸), there were points in it that differed from the Analects (Lunyu 論語). The Analects says, "The Master rarely spoke of destiny and humaneness," and that "his views on human nature and the Way of Heaven cannot be heard"; whereas the Doctrine of the Mean begins by speaking of "what Heaven imparts is called human nature," and says, "Humaneness is what it means to be human," and "Sincerity is the Way of Heaven"—why is this? In the Analects, replying to Zilu's 子路 question about serving ghosts and spirits, he said, "When you are not yet able to serve men, how can you serve ghosts?"; whereas the Doctrine of the Mean speaks at great length of the virtue of ghosts and spirits, saying that they "cause all people in the world to fast, purify themselves, and don splendid attire to carry out sacrifices"—why is this as well? The Analects says, "I can speak of the rites of Yin 殷, but Song 宋 does not adequately attest to them," and "If I were to put them to use, I would follow the predecessors"; whereas the Doctrine of the Mean says, "I have studied the rites of Yin, and they are preserved in Song; I have studied the rites of Zhou 周, and now they are in use [in practice], so I follow Zhou"—why are these statements at odds? The Analects says, "Possessing two-thirds of the realm, yet still serving Yin in submission—the virtue of Zhou may indeed be called supreme virtue!"; whereas the Doctrine of the Mean says, "How far-reaching was the filial piety of King Wu 武王! He was skilful at carrying on the aims of his predecessors and skilful at transmitting their enterprises." Now, given that King Wen 文王 served Zhou 紂 his entire life, while King Wu attacked and overthrew him before a single morning was out, how can this be called skilfully carrying on his aims and transmitting his enterprises? The Analects refers to the Master as "Master" (Zi 子), whereas the Doctrine of the Mean refers to him as "Zhongni 仲尼"—how could a grandson refer to his grandfather by his style name? All of these points cannot but give rise to doubt. Former Confucians said that the Doctrine of the Mean is the method of the mind (xinfa 心法) transmitted within the Confucian school; what…

title: 景泰五年會試錄
text:
所見歟夫既謂之心法矣又何不同
是歟願相與辯之
問古者教人為學之法不外乎大學大學
之書脩己治人之術備矣學者盖求所
以明其道行其道而已學不由於大學
固非正學治不出於大學亦非善治此
自然之理也自唐虞三代以来達而在
上任君師之責者多矣宜皆能躬行是
道以為治也而其間有純乎此者有庶
幾乎此者有悖乎此者先儒盖嘗言之
固可指其人歟窮而在下為聖為賢者
亦多矣宜皆能推明是道以示人也而
其間有取先王之法以詔後世者有作
為傳義以發其意者有畧知乎此而不
求其至者有不務乎此而徒以政教法
令為事者先儒亦嘗言之矣亦可知其
人耶夫明之固欲其行之宋諸大儒非
不明於正學然有嘗表章是書而發其

所見歟？夫既謂之心法矣，又何不同是歟？願相與辯之。
問：古者教人為學之法，不外乎《大學》。《大學》之書，脩己治人之術備矣。學者盖求所以明其道、行其道而已。學不由於《大學》，固非正學；治不出於《大學》，亦非善治，此自然之理也。自唐、虞、三代以来，達而在上，任君師之責者多矣，宜皆能躬行是道以為治也；而其間有純乎此者，有庶幾乎此者，有悖乎此者，先儒盖嘗言之，固可指其人歟？窮而在下，為聖為賢者亦多矣，宜皆能推明是道以示人也；而其間有取先王之法以詔後世者，有作為傳義以發其意者，有畧知乎此而不求其至者，有不務乎此而徒以政教法令為事者，先儒亦嘗言之矣，亦可知其人耶？夫明之固欲其行之，宋諸大儒非不明於正學，然有嘗表章是書而發其
translation_en:
…was their basis for seeing it so? Moreover, since it is called the transmission of the Way of the Mind, how then could there be such discrepancies as these? I wish to examine and distinguish these points with you.
Question: In antiquity, the method of teaching people how to pursue learning did not go beyond the Great Learning (Daxue). In the book of the Great Learning, the arts of cultivating oneself and governing others are complete. Scholars simply seek the means to illuminate its Way and practice its Way, and nothing more. Learning that does not proceed from the Great Learning is certainly not orthodox learning; governance that does not issue from the Great Learning is likewise not good governance. This is a natural principle. Since the time of Tang, Yu, and the Three Dynasties, there have been many who achieved eminence above and bore the responsibilities of ruler and teacher. All of them ought to have been able to personally practice this Way in order to govern; yet among them there were those who were purely devoted to this, those who came close to this, and those who ran counter to this. Former Confucians have spoken of them—can you point out who those men were? There have also been many who remained in obscurity below as sages and worthies. All of them ought to have been able to elucidate this Way in order to show it to others; yet among them there were those who took the methods of the former kings to instruct later generations, those who composed commentary and exposition to bring out its meaning, those who had a rough knowledge of this without seeking its ultimate perfection, and those who did not devote themselves to this at all but occupied themselves solely with administrative instruction and legal ordinances. Former Confucians have also spoken of them—can we know who those men were as well? Now, illuminating it is surely undertaken out of a desire to put it into practice. The great Confucian masters of the Song dynasty were by no means unclear about orthodox learning; yet although some singled out and honored this book to reveal its…

title: 景泰五年會試錄
text:
歸趣亦有采輯是書而進講於其君動
以誠意為言者而皆不能成至治於當
時何也諸士子學大學者也必熟於此
願相與明之
問書臯陶謨有曰在知人在安民斯二者
誠經世之要當今之急務也奚可以不
講耶國以民為本也若何而能使民安
其業無飢寒之患有禮讓之風歟民以
吏而治也若何而能使吏稱其職有循
===
良之風無貪黷之行歟教養之政所以
為民也今農桑非不舉而衣食之資或
不足學校非不脩而禮讓之風猶未興
果何道而能使民家給人足而風移俗
易歟勸懲之典所以為吏也今爵賞非
不厚而循良之政或未聞刑罰非不嚴
而貪墨之風猶自若果何法而能使吏
皆守法奉公而循良愷悌歟之二端謂
政不繫於是耶則古人由之以治謂必

…ultimate purport, and there were also those who compiled material on this book and lectured upon it before their sovereign, speaking constantly of making the intentions sincere—yet none of them were able to achieve supreme governance in their own time. Why was this? You scholars are students of the Great Learning (Daxue) and must be well versed in this; I wish to elucidate it together with you.
Question: In the "Counsels of Gao Yao" (Gao Yao mo) of the Book of Documents (Shu), it is said: "It lies in knowing men; it lies in giving peace to the people." These two things are truly the essentials of statecraft and the urgent tasks of the present day; how could they not be discussed? The state takes the people as its foundation. How can one cause the people to be content in their occupations, free from the distress of hunger and cold, and possessed of customs of propriety and deference? The people are governed through officials. How can one cause officials to be equal to their duties, possessed of the air of law-abiding and upright administrators, and free from greedy and corrupt conduct? Policies of instruction and nourishment are meant for the sake of the people. Today, agriculture and sericulture are not unpromoted, yet resources for food and clothing are at times insufficient; schools are not unmaintained, yet customs of propriety and deference have still not arisen. By what Way, indeed, can one cause every household to be provided for and every person well supplied, so that customs are transformed? The statutes of encouragement and punishment are meant for the sake of officials. Today, noble ranks and rewards are not ungenerous, yet upright and benevolent administration is at times unheard of; punishments and penalties are not unstrict, yet greedy and corrupt customs remain as before. By what method, indeed, can one cause officials all to abide by the law, devote themselves to the public good, and be upright, benevolent, and genial? As for these two matters, if one says that governance does not depend upon them, yet the ancients achieved order by means of them; if one says that it certainly…

title: 景泰五年會試錄
text:
繫於是耶則今者行之未效豈宜於古
而不宜於今歟抑奉行者未得其道歟
諸士子博古通今於經世之術講之有
素矣其悉心以對
問周典六卿政官謂之司馬盖以馬者政
之所重兵旅所恃以取勝者也當是時
校人掌王馬之政辨六馬之属所謂六
馬可指其名歟其養良馬有三乘三皁
六繫六廏可辨其等歟有圉有師有趣
===
馬有馭夫有僕夫有左右校何所隸歟
說者謂古今馬政不同周以官民通牧
漢以民牧而用於官唐以官牧而用於
民宋之時始牧於官後畜於民又其後
市於戎狄其得失可考而言歟方
今監寺有馬郡邑有馬是即成周官民通牧
之意也然牧於官者民給芻秣牧於民
者官責孳償無乃以是而困民歟伊欲
民不困而馬益蕃足以壮兵旅而却寇

問：周典六卿，政官謂之司馬。盖以馬者，政之所重，兵旅所恃以取勝者也。當是時，校人掌王馬之政，辨六馬之属。所謂六馬，可指其名歟？其養良馬，有三乘、三皁、六繫、六廏，可辨其等歟？有圉、有師、有趣馬、有馭夫、有僕夫、有左右校，何所隸歟？說者謂古今馬政不同：周以官民通牧；漢以民牧而用於官；唐以官牧而用於民；宋之時，始牧於官，後畜於民，又其後市於戎狄。其得失可考而言歟？方今監寺有馬，郡邑有馬，是即成周官民通牧之意也。然牧於官者，民給芻秣；牧於民者，官責孳償，無乃以是而困民歟？伊欲民不困而馬益蕃，足以壮兵旅而却寇
translation_en:
…depend upon these? Then today we practice them, yet without effect. Is it that they were suited to antiquity and not suited to the present? Or is it that those who implement them have not yet grasped the proper way? You scholars are well-versed in both antiquity and the present, and have long studied the arts of statecraft; reply with all your hearts.

Question: In the institutions of Zhou, among the Six Ministers, the Minister of Governance was called the Minister of War (Sima). This was because horses were what governance valued most heavily, and what military forces relied upon to achieve victory. At that time, the Commandant of the Royal Stables (Jiaoren) had charge of the administration of the king's horses and distinguished the categories of the six kinds of horses. Can you point out the names of what were called the six kinds of horses? In rearing fine horses, there were three teams of four (cheng), three stalls of twelve (zao), six hitching-lines (xi), and six stables (jiu); can you distinguish their grades? There were grooms (yu), stable masters (shi), stable attendants (zouma), chariot-drivers (yufu), carriage-servants (pufu), and the directors of the left and right enclosures (zuoyou xiao); to whom were they subordinate? Commentators say that horse administration has differed from antiquity to the present: the Zhou Pastured horses jointly through officials and the people; the Han had the people pasture them for use by the officials; the Tang had the officials pasture them for use by the people; and in the time of the Song, they were first pastured by the officials, later raised among the people, and still later purchased from the northern and western frontier tribes (Rong and Di). Can their successes and failures be examined and stated? At present, the directorates and courts have horses, and the prefectures and counties have horses; this is indeed the intent of the joint official and popular pasturing of the flourishing Zhou. Yet for those pastured by the officials, the people supply fodder and grain; and for those pastured by the people, the officials demand breeding quotas and compensation for losses—does this not burden the people on that account? Four Books

"The Master standing by a stream, said, 'It passes on just like this, not ceasing day or night!'"

Zhuo Tianxi 卓天錫

Associate Examiner Secretary Zhang 章 comments: Most candidates writing on this topic use the flowing stream as a metaphor for the substance of the Way, which quite misses the original purport. This essay is able to thoroughly grasp its meaning, and the wording suffices to bring it out; the author must be someone well-versed in the Learning of Principle (lixue 理學).
Associate Examiner Senior Compiler Ke 柯 comments: The flowing stream is what is visible within the inherent state of the substance of the Way, which the Sage specially pointed to in order to show others. Most writers are blind to this meaning; only this piece is able to synthesize the commentaries into an essay, and its conclusion is especially apt—most commendable, most commendable!
Examiner Librarian Li 李 comments: In this essay, the understanding of principle is clear and the phrasing is concise and to the point. Works like this in the examination hall are rarely seen; it ought to be placed in the front ranks.
Examiner Academician Shang 商 comments: Those in the examination hall writing explications on the Analects (Lunyu 論語) all produce specious words; an intimate and personal grasp of the truth is seen only in this piece.

The Sage, perceiving something through that in which it inheres, sighed over the inexhaustibility of the substance of the Way. Now, the flowing stream shares its substance with the Way; the unceasingness of the flowing stream is the unceasingness of the substance of the Way. Having perceived this, how could the Sage not express it in order to show others? Why is this so? In the transformations of Heaven and Earth, what departs passes by and what comes continues, without a single moment's pause—this is the inherent state of the substance of the Way. Yet among things that can be pointed to and easily seen, none compares to a flowing stream. text:
行也有如是夫蓋自水之往而過者觀之滔滔而逝
不以晝夜而或止則道體之往而過者於是乎在焉
自水之来而續者觀之源源而至不以旦夕而或息
則道體之来而續者於此乎見焉道無形也而寓於有
形之水水有形也而載乎無形之道即此而觀則道
在天地間曷嘗有一息之間哉夫子指以示人其欲
學者時時省察而加夫自強不息之功也歟抑論之
盈穹壤間皆道也而川流特其一端耳故子思子於
中庸以鳶魚之飛躍明斯道之昭著殆與此同一機

行也，有如是夫！蓋自水之往而過者觀之，滔滔而逝，不以晝夜而或止，則道體之往而過者，於是乎在焉；自水之来而續者觀之，源源而至，不以旦夕而或息，則道體之来而續者，於此乎見焉。道無形也，而寓於有形之水；水有形也，而載乎無形之道。即此而觀，則道在天地間，曷嘗有一息之間哉？夫子指以示人，其欲學者時時省察，而加夫自強不息之功也歟？抑論之，盈穹壤間皆道也，而川流特其一端耳。故子思子於《中庸》，以鳶魚之飛躍，明斯道之昭著，殆與此同一機也。然川流有以見道之無時不然，鳶魚飛躍則以見道之無物不有，此又體道者所當知。

translation_en:
…courses on is just like this! For if we observe it from the waters that pass by and go on, surging away without ever stopping day or night, then the passing and going on of the substance of the Way resides right there; if we observe it from the waters that come and continue, arriving in an unbroken stream without ever ceasing morning or evening, then the coming and continuing of the substance of the Way is seen right here. The Way is formless, yet it lodges in water, which has form; water has form, yet it carries the formless Way. Observed from this, when has the Way between heaven and earth ever had a single breath of interruption? When the Master pointed this out to show others, did he not wish learners to examine themselves at all times and apply the effort of unceasing self-strengthening? Moreover, if we discuss it further, filling the expanse between heaven and earth, all is the Way, and a flowing stream is merely one aspect of it. Thus Master Zisi, in the Doctrine of the Mean (Zhongyong), used the flying of kites and leaping of fishes to elucidate the manifest brilliance of this Way, which shares nearly the same pivotal principle as this. Yet a flowing stream serves to show that there is no time when the Way is not so, whereas the flying of kites and leaping of fishes serve to show that there is no thing in which the Way is not present—this too is what those who embody the Way ought to know.

考試官學士商批說分田制祿及厚君子野
人處明白可觀
大賢勸滕之君臣既欲隨地而分田以制祿又欲因
人而授田以加厚夫分田制祿所以治野人使養君
子也然不於常法之外而有加焉其何以厚於君子
野人哉昔孟子因滕君使其臣畢戰問井地而以分
田制祿之法告之若曰滕國雖小亦必有為君子而仕
===
者有為野人而耕者則分田制祿之法豈可偏廢哉
是故野為郊門之外都鄙之地田可井授也則請
行九一而助之法焉九一而助則都鄙用助法而
公田所入有以為君子之祿矣國中郊門之內鄉遂
之地田不井授也則使什分稅一而自賦於上焉什一
自賦則鄉遂用貢法而賦之所入有以充國家之用矣
此分田所以給野人而制祿所以待君子也然於常法之
外豈無所當加厚者哉夫自卿以下至於大夫固有常
祿矣然有田斯可祭也故必加以圭田五十畝使得潔

公田所入有以爲君子之祿矣國中郊門之內鄉遂
之地田不井授也則使什分稅一而自賦於上焉什一
自賦則鄉遂用貢法而賦之所入有以充國家之用矣
此分田所以給野人而制祿所以待君子也然於常法之
外豈無所當加厚者哉夫自卿以下至於大夫固有常
祿矣然有田斯可盡祭也故必加以圭田五十畝使得潔
punctuated:
多失之泛，此篇議論切實，宜表而出之。
考試官洗馬李批：文字整齊，不泛不畧，可取。
考試官學士商批：說分田制祿及厚君子、野人處，明白可觀。

大賢勸滕之君臣，既欲隨地而分田以制祿，又欲因人而授田以加厚。夫分田制祿，所以治野人使養君子也；然不於常法之外而有加焉，其何以厚於君子、野人哉？昔孟子因滕君使其臣畢戰問井地，而以分田制祿之法告之，若曰：滕國雖小，亦必有為君子而仕者，有為野人而耕者，則分田制祿之法豈可偏廢哉？是故野為郊門之外、都鄙之地，田可井授也，則請行九一而助之法焉。九一而助，則都鄙用助法，而公田所入有以為君子之祿矣。國中郊門之內、鄉遂之地，田不井授也，則使什分稅一而自賦於上焉。什一自賦，則鄉遂用貢法，而賦之所入有以充國家之用矣。此分田所以給野人，而制祿所以待君子也。然於常法之外，豈無所當加厚者哉？夫自卿以下至於大夫，固有常祿矣；然有田斯可祭也，故必加以圭田五十畝，使得潔

…mostly erred on the side of vagueness. The discussion in this piece is concrete and substantive; it should be singled out for distinction.
Examiner and Librarian of the Left Secretariat of the Heir Apparent Li comments: The composition is well-ordered, neither vague nor cursory; it is worthy of selection.
Examiner and Hanlin Academician Shang comments: The explanation of the passages on dividing the fields, establishing emoluments, and treating both the gentlemen and the rustics generously is clear and impressive.

In urging the ruler and minister of Teng, the Great Worthy wished both to divide the fields according to the terrain so as to establish emoluments, and to grant additional fields according to the individuals so as to show generous treatment. Now, dividing the fields and establishing emoluments are the means by which one governs the rustics and causes them to support the gentlemen; yet if nothing were added beyond the regular statutes, how could one treat the gentlemen and the rustics generously? Formerly, when the ruler of Teng sent his minister Bi Zhan to inquire about the well-field system, Mencius informed him of the method of dividing the fields and establishing emoluments, as if to say: Although the state of Teng is small, there must also be those who act as gentlemen and serve in office, and those who act as rustics and till the soil; how, then, could either aspect of the method of dividing the fields and establishing emoluments be neglected? Therefore, in the countryside—the territory of the outer towns and borderlands beyond the suburban gates—where the fields can be granted in well-field grids, I request that you implement the one-in-nine mutual-aid system. With the one-in-nine mutual-aid system, the outer towns and borderlands use the mutual-aid method, and the revenue from the public fields provides the emoluments for the gentlemen. Within the capital—the territory of the metropolitan districts and outer districts inside the suburban gates—where the fields are not granted in well-field grids, have them pay a tax of one part in ten and contribute it themselves to their superiors. With a self-contributed tithe, the metropolitan and outer districts use the tribute method, and the revenue from the levy suffices to supply the needs of the state. Thus, dividing the fields is the means to provide for the rustics, and establishing emoluments is the means to treat the gentlemen. Yet beyond the regular statutes, how could there not be cases where additional generosity is due? From the Chief Ministers down to the Grand Masters, they naturally have their regular emoluments; yet only when one possesses fields can one perform sacrifices, and so they must be granted an additional fifty mou of sacrificial fields, allowing them to…

易
「九五：觀我生，君子無咎。《象》曰：觀我生，觀民也。」
同考試官給事中王批：題本平易，作者多體認戒辭不出。此篇辭簡理明，盖精於《易》者，宜表而出之。

translation_en:
…pure and abundant offerings so as to fulfill the rites of sacrificing to their ancestors. An individual householder supporting his parents above and his wife and children below certainly has his regular property; yet if he has younger brothers, these are "surplus householders" (yufu), and they must further be granted twenty-five mu of land for a surplus householder, waiting until they come of age and take a wife, after which they are separately allotted a field of one hundred mu. This is how, beyond the regular system of hereditary emoluments, gentlemen are treated generously, and how, beyond the regular system of one hundred mu, countryfolk are treated generously. Ah! When a ruler governs a state, if toward both gentlemen and countryfolk he not only has the means to nourish them, but also has the means to treat them generously, is this not the greatest of benevolent governance? Furthermore, if we consider that during the Warring States period the well-field system had broken down and the feudal lords had all gotten rid of its registers, only the learning of Mencius grasped its great principles. Therefore, in his counsel to Duke Wen and Bi Zhan, he was able to proceed from the rough outline to arrive at the details, and to extend the old to make it new—not getting bogged down in the traces of the past, yet able to accord with the intentions of the former kings. Truly, he may be called a world-renowned talent of the Second Sage!

Book of Changes (Yi)
"Nine in the Fifth Place: Contemplating my own life, the superior man is without fault. The Commentary on the Images (Xiang) says: 'Contemplating my own life' means contemplating the people."
Comment by Associate Examiner Supervising Secretary Wang: The topic itself is plain and straightforward, yet most writers failed to grasp and bring out the admonitory words. This essay is concise in diction and clear in principle; it is surely by one well-versed in the Book of Changes, and ought to be singled out for distinction.
Comment by Associate Examiner Expositor-in-waiting Yang: Fine essays on the Book of Changes are certainly numerous, but when we came upon this composition, its diction and conception were lofty and pure, like a crimson [?] suddenly emerging amid a thicket of yellow and white [?], catching the eye.

title: 景泰五年會試錄
text:
考試官洗馬李批以本諸身徵諸民立說正
合題意宜在所選
考試官學士商批此篇發明君子為觀之道
深合本義
居尊而為衆所仰爻以本諸身戒其占象以徵諸民申
其義盖人君為觀於天下固當觀己所行以補其過
也然不觀夫民德之善否將何以察己之得失哉是
宜爻象聖人有以各極其旨也今夫觀之九五以陽
剛中正之德履崇高富貴之位在下四陰仰而觀之
===
為大觀之主有君子之象也居是位而得是占者宜
何如哉必也反觀內省亦如九五之陽剛不為陰柔
之所侵視履考祥亦如九五之中正不為憸邪之所
惑則合乎君子之道而得乎大君之宜果何過咎之
有爻戒其占如此吾夫子於象又以義言之謂夫人
君政化之得失係乎民臣之從違也故欲觀一己之
所為孰若觀諸民心以自省察乎治道之隆替關乎
風俗之媺惡也故欲察一身之所行孰若察諸民俗
以自克治乎是所謂徵諸庶民也是所謂當於民監

爲大觀之主有君子之象也居是位而得是占者宜
何如哉必也反觀内省亦如九五之陽剛不爲陰柔
之所侵視履考祥亦如九五之中正不爲憸邪之所

有爻戒其占如此吾夫子於象□以義言之謂夫人
君政化之得失係乎民臣之從違也故欲觀一己之
所爲孰若觀諸民心以自省察乎治道之隆替關乎
風俗之媺惡也故欲察一身之所行孰若察諸民俗
以自克治乎是所謂徵諸庶民也是所謂當於民監
punctuated:
考試官洗馬李批：以「本諸身，徵諸民」立說，正合題意，宜在所選。
考試官學士商批：此篇發明君子為觀之道，深合《本義》。
居尊而為衆所仰，爻以「本諸身」戒其占，象以「徵諸民」申其義。盖人君為觀於天下，固當觀己所行以補其過也；然不觀夫民德之善否，將何以察己之得失哉？是宜爻、象聖人有以各極其旨也。今夫《觀》之九五，以陽剛中正之德，履崇高富貴之位，在下四陰仰而觀之，為大觀之主，有君子之象也。居是位而得是占者，宜何如哉？必也反觀內省，亦如九五之陽剛，不為陰柔之所侵；視履考祥，亦如九五之中正，不為憸邪之所惑。則合乎君子之道，而得乎大君之宜，果何過咎之有？爻戒其占如此。吾夫子於《象》又以義言之，謂夫人君政化之得失，係乎民臣之從違也，故欲觀一己之所為，孰若觀諸民心以自省察乎？治道之隆替，關乎風俗之媺惡也，故欲察一身之所行，孰若察諸民俗以自克治乎？是所謂「徵諸庶民」也，是所謂「當於民監」
translation_en:
Examiner Li, Librarian in the Establishment of the Heir Apparent, comments: Setting forth the argument on the basis of "rooting it in one's own person and verifying it among the people" precisely matches the meaning of the theme; it ought to be among those selected.
Examiner Shang, Hanlin Academician, comments: This essay elucidates the Way by which the noble man serves as an example to be observed, deeply according with the Original Meaning (Benyi).
Occupying the position of honor and looked up to by the multitude, the line statement admonishes the diviner with "rooting it in one's own person," while the Commentary on the Images (Xiang) extends its meaning with "verifying it among the people." Indeed, when a ruler serves as an example to be observed by all under heaven, he ought of course to observe his own conduct in order to remedy his faults. Yet if he does not observe whether the virtue of the people is good or bad, how shall he examine his own successes and failures? It is fitting, therefore, that in the line statement and the Commentary on the Images the sages each exhausted the full import of the matter. Now, the nine in the fifth place of the hexagram Guan [Contemplation], possessing the virtue of yang firmness, centrality, and correctness, treads the position of exalted eminence, wealth, and honor; the four yin lines below look up and observe him, so that he is the lord of great contemplation and has the image of a noble man. For one who occupies this position and obtains this divination, how ought he to act? Surely he must look inward and examine himself, being, like the nine in the fifth place in its yang firmness, unencroached upon by yin softness; he must examine his path and scrutinize its auspices, being, like the nine in the fifth place in its centrality and correctness, undeluded by artful evil. Then he will accord with the Way of the noble man and attain what is fitting for a great ruler—what fault or blame could there indeed be? Such is the admonition that the line statement gives for the divination. Our Master [Confucius], in the Commentary on the Images, further spoke of it in terms of its moral principle, holding that the success or failure of a ruler's governance and transformation depends upon the compliance or defiance of his subjects and people; therefore, if he wishes to observe what he himself does, how can that compare to observing the minds of the people so as to examine himself? The flourishing or decline of the Way of governance is bound up with the beauty or ugliness of customs and mores; therefore, if he wishes to examine what he himself practices, how can that compare to examining the customs of the people so as to discipline and govern himself? This is what is meant by "verifying it among the common people"; this is what is meant by "one ought to take the people as a mirror"…

translation_en:
… The Commentary on the Images (Xiang) further elaborates its meaning in this way. Yet if we examine the appended line texts, why is it that the Sage already says at the Fifth Line, "contemplating my own life," and then at the Top Nine again says, "contemplating his life," followed by the very same admonition? It is because in this hexagram there are only two yang lines, and both are looked up to by the multitude of yin lines. Top Nine is yang and firm, residing above the position of honor without holding the responsibility of affairs; therefore, its words of admonition are roughly the same as those for the Fifth Line, merely changing "my" (wo) to "his" (qi), with a slight distinction between host and guest. Scholars must not fail to know this.

"When the clans of the Yellow Emperor (Huangdi), Yao, and Shun arose, they carried through the changes so that the people did not grow weary; they spirit-like transformed them so that the people found them fitting. In the Changes (Yi), when a thing reaches its limit, it changes; changing, it passes through; passing through, it endures. Therefore, 'Help comes to him from Heaven; there is good fortune and nothing that is not beneficial.' The Yellow Emperor, Yao, and Shun let their upper and lower garments hang down and the world was well governed: this they probably took from the hexagrams Qian and Kun."
By Duan Jian 段堅.

Associate Examiner Supervising Secretary Wang comments: Writers in the examination hall treated this superficially and missed the mark. This essay threads together the main purport of carrying through changes and suiting the people; its diction is concise and its reasoning clear, so it deserves to be placed among the selected.
Associate Examiner Expositor-in-waiting Yang comments: Although the topic is long, many candidates had also anticipated and practiced it; yet the difficulty lies not in composing an essay on it, but in assimilating its meaning without being verbose or derivative. This piece comes close indeed!
Examiner Librarian Li comments: The arrangement and exposition of this piece are concise and apt; it is worthy of selection.
Examiner Academician Shang comments: The sages' carrying through of changes and governing by non-action were simply in accordance with their times…

title: 景泰五年會試錄
text:
耳此作得之
聖人迭興變通之妙合於易者得乎天無為之象著
於民者契乎易夫隨時致治自合乎易之道也變通
无為聖人既各因時而為之則得乎天而著于民者
又豈不合乎易道也哉昔者風氣漸開之時備物致
用之日黄帝作於前堯舜繼於後易負戴而為舟車
變巢穴而為宫室是其時之不可以不變也可變而
變民心翕從但見為之不倦行之不勞茫乎如神之
化民之宜於出入養生自若也聖人有為如此豈无
===
自而然哉盖體乎易之變通也易之道天之道也易

乎易通其變而後能久聖人神化以契乎易天豈不

不過垂衣裳而已衣垂於上而尊貴之象著裳垂於

punctuated:
耳，此作得之。

聖人迭興，變通之妙合於《易》者，得乎天；無為之象著於民者，契乎《易》。夫隨時致治，自合乎《易》之道也。變通无為，聖人既各因時而為之，則得乎天而著于民者，又豈不合乎《易》道也哉？昔者風氣漸開之時，備物致用之日，黄帝作於前，堯、舜繼於後，易負戴而為舟車，變巢穴而為宫室，是其時之不可以不變也。可變而變，民心翕從，但見為之不倦，行之不勞，茫乎如神之化，民之宜於出入養生自若也。聖人有為如此，豈无自而然哉？盖體乎《易》之變通也。《易》之道，天之道也。《易》窮於陽，變而通陰；聖人變通以合《易》，天豈不錫以福乎？《易》通其變而後能久；聖人神化以契乎《易》，天豈不祐以吉乎？夫民從之而天祐之，聖人斯時復何為哉？不過垂衣裳而已。衣垂於上，而尊貴之象著；裳垂於下，而卑賤之象彰。藹然文物而大變其蚩蠢之俗，善乾道變化而生物也；燁然衣冠而大變其敦龐之風，若坤道承天而成物也。聖人治世无為，而合乎乾坤變化如此，抑豈容心於其間哉？不過因時制宜而已。
translation_en:
… only; this composition has grasped it.

As the sages arose in succession, the subtlety of their adaptations and transformations, conforming to the Book of Changes (Yi), obtained the favor of Heaven; the emblem of their non-purposive action, manifested among the people, tallied with the Book of Changes. Indeed, bringing about order in accordance with the times naturally conforms to the Way of the Changes. Since the sages each practiced adaptation and non-action in response to their times, how could that which obtained the favor of Heaven and was manifested among the people not also conform to the Way of the Changes?

In antiquity, when civilization was gradually opening up and things were being prepared for practical use, the Yellow Emperor (Huangdi) arose beforehand and Yao and Shun succeeded him afterward. They replaced carrying loads on the back and head with boats and carriages, and transformed nests and caves into houses and palaces—this was because the times could not but change. When change was called for and they made changes, the hearts of the people harmoniously followed. One saw only that they acted without weariness and put things into practice without toil; vast and boundless like a spiritual transformation, the people found convenience in going out, coming in, and nourishing their lives quite naturally. When the sages took action like this, how could it have been so without a source? For they embodied the adaptations and transformations of the Changes. The Way of the Changes is the Way of Heaven. In the Changes, when yang reaches its limit, it changes and passes through to yin; when the sages adapted and transformed to conform with the Changes, how could Heaven not bestow blessings upon them? The Changes passes through its transformations and only then can endure; when the sages wrought spiritual transformations to tally with the Changes, how could Heaven not assist them with good fortune?

Now, with the people following them and Heaven assisting them, what more did the sages have to do at that time? They merely let their upper and lower garments hang down, and nothing more. With the upper garment hanging above, the emblem of the noble and exalted was made manifest; with the lower garment hanging below, the emblem of the humble and lowly was made clear. Flourishing were the rites and institutions, greatly transforming the ignorant and simple customs, just as [reading 善 as 若] the Way of Qian changes and transforms to give birth to things; brilliant were the robes and caps, greatly transforming the plain and unadorned manners, just as the Way of Kun receives from Heaven to bring things to completion. That the sages governed the world through non-action and yet conformed to the changes and transformations of Qian and Kun like this—how could they have harbored any deliberate calculation therein? They merely instituted what was appropriate in accordance with the times, and nothing more.

translation_en:
Furthermore, if we discuss adapting and changing in accordance with the times, was this true only of the Yellow Emperor, Yao, and Shun? Consider how the Xia dynasty esteemed loyalty—it was not that this was not good, yet the Shang changed it by turning to simplicity. The Shang esteemed simplicity—it was not that this was not good, yet the Zhou changed it by turning to refinement. This too was nothing more than changing in accordance with the times. If students of the Book of Changes (Yi) examine these together, it will be sufficient to understand the sages' way of adaptation and change.

"When I err, you shall correct me; you shall not comply to my face and after retiring speak otherwise behind my back. Reverently attend to the four neighboring associates."

title: 景泰五年會試錄
text:
當是作者
聖君命大臣既欲盡弼直之道尤欲敬為隣之職盖
人臣進言不可以不直而任職不可以不敬聖君以
是責望大臣何其至哉昔帝舜申弼直隣哉之義而
責之禹若曰臣者君之輔也弼直之謨爾固告我矣
弼直之義容可不盡乎我於政教之行有戾於道也
爾當繩愆糾繆以弼正其失爾無面諛以為合乎道
而退以為非道焉我於禮樂之施有悖於理也爾當
面折廷諍以規正其非爾無阿徇以為當乎理而退
===
以為非理焉且爾之於我以人言則為臣以職言則
為隣臣哉隣哉我已属望於爾矣爾可不兢兢焉敬
爾左右輔弼之任乎隣哉臣哉我已委重於爾矣爾
可不業業焉敬爾股肱耳目之職乎盖盡其弼直之
道則事上無欺心敬其為隣之職則處己無怠心大
臣之義盡於此矣雖然舜聖君也豈有違待於弼禹
聖臣也豈有面從後言而猶諄諄及此此其不自以
為聖也厥後禹之告舜至曰無若丹朱好慢遊作傲
虐則所以儆戒之者為何如哉有虞君臣交相責難

punctuated:
當是作者。
聖君命大臣，既欲盡弼直之道，尤欲敬為隣之職。盖人臣進言不可以不直，而任職不可以不敬，聖君以是責望大臣，何其至哉！昔帝舜申「弼直」、「隣哉」之義而責之禹，若曰：臣者，君之輔也。「弼直」之謨，爾固告我矣，弼直之義，容可不盡乎？我於政教之行，有戾於道也，爾當繩愆糾繆，以弼正其失；爾無面諛以為合乎道，而退以為非道焉。我於禮樂之施，有悖於理也，爾當面折廷諍，以規正其非；爾無阿徇以為當乎理，而退以為非理焉。且爾之於我，以人言則為臣，以職言則為隣。「臣哉隣哉」，我已属望於爾矣，爾可不兢兢焉敬爾左右輔弼之任乎？「隣哉臣哉」，我已委重於爾矣，爾可不業業焉敬爾股肱耳目之職乎？盖盡其弼直之道，則事上無欺心；敬其為隣之職，則處己無怠心。大臣之義，盡於此矣。雖然，舜，聖君也，豈有違待於弼？禹，聖臣也，豈有面從後言？而猶諄諄及此，此其不自以為聖也。厥後禹之告舜，至曰：「無若丹朱，好慢遊，作傲虐。」則所以儆戒之者為何如哉！有虞君臣交相責難，
translation_en:
… This must be the work of an accomplished writer.

When the sage ruler charged his great minister, he not only wished him to fulfill the way of assisting toward rectitude, but even more wished him to be reverent in his office as a close associate. For in offering counsel, a minister cannot fail to be forthright, and in discharging his office, he cannot fail to be reverent. How utmost were the expectations that the sage ruler placed upon his great minister in this regard!

Of old, when Emperor Shun reiterated the meaning of "assisting toward rectitude" and "being a close associate" in charging Yu, it was as if he said: "A minister is the assistant to his ruler. You have indeed already imparted to me the counsel of 'assisting toward rectitude'; how, then, can the duty of assisting toward rectitude not be fulfilled to the utmost? If, in my implementation of governance and instruction, there is anything contrary to the Way, you must correct faults and rectify errors so as to assist in setting right my failings; you must not flatter me to my face as being in accord with the Way, and then after withdrawing say that it is contrary to the Way. If, in my institution of rites and music, there is anything that violates principle, you must rebuke me to my face and remonstrate at court so as to admonish and correct my wrongs; you must not pander and comply as if it were consistent with principle, and then after withdrawing say that it is contrary to principle. Moreover, in your relation to me, spoken of in terms of person, you are a minister; spoken of in terms of office, you are a close associate. 'Be a minister! Be my close associate!'—I have already placed my hopes in you; how can you not be cautiously reverent toward your responsibility of assisting me at my left and right? 'Be my close associate! Be a minister!'—I have already entrusted heavy responsibilities to you; how can you not be vigilantly reverent toward your office as my limbs, eyes, and ears?"

Indeed, to fulfill the way of assisting toward rectitude means serving one's superior without a deceitful heart; to be reverent in the office of a close associate means conducting oneself without a negligent heart. The duty of a great minister is exhausted in this. Even so, Shun was a sage ruler—how could he have had transgressions waiting to be corrected? Yu was a sage minister—how could he have complied to his face and spoken otherwise behind his back? Yet Shun still spoke of this with such earnest repetition; this was because they did not regard themselves as sages. Later, when Yu counseled Shun, he went so far as to say: "Do not be like Danzhu, who loved idle wandering and committed arrogant cruelty." How profound, then, was the admonition and warning he offered! How ruler and minister in the虞 (Yu) dynasty held one another to the highest standards…

translation_en:
… can be seen in this.

"Yu then succeeded and rose up, and Heaven thereupon bestowed on Yu the Great Plan (Hongfan) in nine categories, whereby the constant human relationships were set in order. The first is called the Five Phases; the second is called the reverent practice of the Five Personal Matters; the third is called the earnest application of the EightMeasures of Government; the fourth is called the harmonious use of the Five Regulators of Time; the fifth is called the establishment and use of Supreme Perfection; the sixth is called the governing application of the Three Virtues; the seventh is called the intelligent use of the Examination of Doubts; the eighth is called the thoughtful attention to the Various Verifications; the ninth is called the encouragement through the Five Blessings and the deterrence through the Six Extremities."

By Tu Fei 涂𤩽.

Associate Examiner Director Zhang comments: Among those in the examination hall who wrote on this topic, the elaborate ones certainly erred on the side of diffuseness, while the concise ones erred on the side of sketchiness. text:
聖人第其疇而治道備盖數之所在理之所在也非上
天畀是數於聖人則常道何由而明非聖人因是數
而第疇則治道何由而備哉昔者鯀湮洪水九載弗
績大禹継出厥功有成於是天不愛道錫之以神龜
之文有數至九禹也因而第之以成九類則大法由
是而著常道以之而明此彝倫之所以叙也彝倫之
叙即九疇之叙也然九疇之所叙果何如哉誠以在
天惟五行在人惟五事故因其數之一而以五行第

… [natural numbers], the sage arranged its divisions in order, and the Way of governance was made complete. For where the numbers reside, there principle resides also. Had High Heaven not bestowed these numbers upon the sage, how could the constant Way have been made clear? Had the sage not followed these numbers to arrange the divisions in order, how could the Way of governance have been made complete?

In antiquity, Gun dammed up the floodwaters, and for nine years failed to achieve results; Great Yu succeeded him and brought the work to completion. Thereupon Heaven did not withhold the Way, bestowing upon him the markings on the sacred tortoise, with numbers reaching up to nine. Yu accordingly arranged them in order so as to form the nine categories; thus the Great Plan was thereby made manifest and the constant Way was through it illuminated—this is how the invariable human relationships were set in order. The ordering of the invariable relationships is none other than the ordering of the Nine Divisions.

Yet what, in truth, is the ordering of the Nine Divisions? Truly, in Heaven there are only the Five Agents, and in man there are only the Five Personal Matters. Therefore, following the number one and arranging it with the Five Agents, water, fire, wood, metal, and earth are everywhere put to use; following the number two and arranging it with the Five Personal Matters, demeanor, speech, sight, hearing, and thought make complete the Way of making one's person sincere. Furthermore, following the number three and arranging it with the Eight Objects of Government—from food and commodities down to guests and the multitude [or army]—is the means to enrich the people's livelihood; following the number four and arranging it with the Five Arrangements of Time—from the year and the month down to the astronomical calculations—is the means to accord with Heaven. Are not these four the basis upon which the substance of the August Ultimate is established?

As for the number five occupying the center and being arranged with the August Ultimate, the ruler thereby has the means to establish the standard of supreme perfection and serve as a model for all under Heaven. Coming to the number six, accordingly arranging it with the Three Virtues—the application of correctness, firmness, and gentleness—is this not the means to govern the people? 古人因飲而致告也既欲謹言而設警懼之詞復慮
過飲而申丁寧之戒蓋言之不謹由飲之無節也古
人於此既設言以恐之又丁寧以戒之其自悔之意
深矣在昔衛武公飲酒悔過而作是詩至是則致告
戒之詞謂夫彼醉不臧怠荒為之也安得從而謂之
俾勿至於大怠乎飲酒伐德媟慢致之也安得從而
===
告之使勿至於媟慢乎告之若曰言合乎理爾則言
之可也於其所不當言則勿言焉語為可從爾則語
之可也於其所不當從則勿語焉苟由醉而妄言則
將罰汝而俾出童羖矣謂之童羖者無角之羖羊必
無之物也設言必無之物以罰其失言之非固足以
使之有所恐矣然猶慮誨爾諄諄而聽我藐藐也故
又丁寧以戒之焉謂爾之飲此旨酒至於三爵已昏
然無所識矣况敢式燕又思而湛樂是從乎爾之稱
彼兕觥至於三酌已冥然無所知矣况敢獻酬交錯

古人因飲而致告也，既欲謹言而設警懼之詞，復慮過飲而申丁寧之戒。蓋言之不謹，由飲之無節也。古人於此，既設言以恐之，又丁寧以戒之，其自悔之意深矣。在昔衛武公飲酒悔過而作是詩，至是則致告戒之詞，謂夫彼醉不臧，怠荒為之也，安得從而謂之，俾勿至於大怠乎？飲酒伐德，媟慢致之也，安得從而告之，使勿至於媟慢乎？告之若曰：言合乎理，爾則言之可也；於其所不當言，則勿言焉。語為可從，爾則語之可也；於其所不當從，則勿語焉。苟由醉而妄言，則將罰汝而俾出童羖矣。謂之童羖者，無角之羖羊，必無之物也。設言必無之物，以罰其失言之非，固足以使之有所恐矣。然猶慮誨爾諄諄，而聽我藐藐也，故又丁寧以戒之焉。謂爾之飲此旨酒，至於三爵，已昏然無所識矣，况敢式燕又思，而湛樂是從乎？爾之稱彼兕觥，至於三酌，已冥然無所知矣，况敢獻酬交錯，
translation_en:
…be among those selected.

Comment by Examiner Academician Shang [Shang Lu 商輅]: This depicts Duke Wu's intention of warning against drinking; its phrasing is gentle yet stern.

When the ancient offered admonition on account of drinking, he not only wished for caution in speech and thus set forth words to alarm and frighten, but also worried about excessive drinking and thus reiterated earnest warnings. For recklessness in speech stems from a lack of restraint in drinking. On this point, the ancient both posited a hypothetical penalty to frighten them and gave earnest injunctions to warn them; his intention of self-repentance was profound indeed.

In antiquity, Duke Wu of Wei (Wei Wugong 衛武公) composed this ode in repentance for faults committed while drinking wine. Coming to this stanza, he delivers words of admonition and warning. He says that when those drunkards behave badly, it is caused by negligence and dissipation—how can one therefore speak to them so as to keep them from reaching extreme negligence? Drinking wine ruins one's virtue, and this is brought about by familiarity and insolence—how can one therefore admonish them so as to keep them from reaching familiarity and insolence?

Admonishing them, it is as if he says: "If words accord with principle, then it is permissible for you to speak them; as for what ought not to be spoken, do not speak it. If discourse is worthy of being followed, then it is permissible for you to utter it; as for what ought not to be followed, do not utter it. If on account of drunkenness you speak recklessly, I shall penalize you by making you produce a hornless ram." What is called a "hornless ram" (tonggu 童羖) is a mature black ram without horns—something that certainly does not exist. Positing something that certainly does not exist in order to penalize the wrong of a slip of the tongue is surely enough to make them feel fear. Yet he still worries that though he instructs them earnestly, they listen to him with indifference; therefore, he again earnestly warns them. He says: "When you drink this fine wine up to three goblets, you are already befuddled and conscious of nothing; how much less should you dare to go on feasting yet again and give yourselves over to steeped pleasure? When you raise that rhinoceros-horn cup up to three draughts, you are already darkened in mind and aware of nothing; how much less should you dare to exchange toasts and pledges back and forth…

考試官□□□批：有周之興，非由人力，實天□□□
translation_en:
… and abandon yourself to wild excess in wine? Alas! That Duke Wu (Wu gong 武公) was so thorough in his admonitions concerning feasting and drinking shows how deeply and earnestly he repented his faults. Furthermore, if we examine the past, when Kang Shu 康叔 was enfeoffed in Wei 衛 at the former capital of Yin 殷, King Wu (Wu wang 武王), because the custom of Yin was given to drunken excess, composed a document to admonish him. Within that single piece, he spoke of virtue eight times and of dignified demeanor once; his intent in admonishing was earnest indeed. Now Duke Wu composed a poem in repentance of his faults, in which he speaks of virtue once and of dignified demeanor five times, mutually complementing the "Announcement about Drunkenness" (Jiu gao 酒誥). Ah! Truly Duke Wu grasped the family traditions of King Wu and Kang Shu!

"God made a state and made a match for Himself, from Taibo 大伯 and Wang Ji 王季."

Yang Ji 楊集

Comment by Associate Examiner, Secretary (zhushi 主事) Zhang 章: The topic is inherently straightforward, yet most writers failed to elucidate it. This essay traces and sets forth the origins of the house of Zhou's receiving the Mandate; its arguments are precise and incisive, not to be compared with the superficial efforts of others.

Comment by Associate Examiner, Senior Compiler (xiuzhuan 脩撰) Ke 柯: This composition threads the word "Heaven" throughout the entire piece, deeply according with the fundamental purport of the passage. Moreover, its literary thought is calm and measured, vividly evoking the spirit of the flourishing of Zhou in those times.

Comment by Examiner, Librarian (xianma 洗馬) Li 李: This essay is able to trace to its source the meaning of Heaven's favor toward Zhou, deeply according with the fundamental purport; it is commendable.

Comment by Examiner […]: The rise of Zhou did not come about through human effort, but truly Heaven […]…

title: 景泰五年會試錄
text:
原上天建國立君之意已定於肇生賢嗣之時甚矣
天眷有周之隆也既建國為興王之地又擇賢為嗣
業之君有周之興豈偶然哉是詩說者以為叙大王
大伯王季之德以及文王伐密伐崇之事也而此章之
意若謂天之眷大王也不惟建國而得其地抑且立君
而得其人觀夫岐山之陽木拔道通有方興未艾之
象是豈人力所能為哉乃天作此興王之邦也地闢
民歸啓周家無窮之業亦豈人力所可致哉乃天建
此興王之國也然不徒作之邦而已又必擇其賢者
===
以當之俾王業有所繼焉不徒建其國而已又必擇
其賢者以君之俾統緒有所承焉天為有周建國立
君之意如此果何所自哉盖自初生大伯王季之時
而已定矣故大伯承大王之志而讓其國人皆以為
天意之所存也殊不知上天眷命已定於初生大伯
之日而不在於讓國之時其讓國也特以成天意爾
王季受大伯之讓而篤其慶人皆以為天心之所在
也殊不知天命降監已定於篤生王季之初而非肇
於受讓之際其受讓也特以順天心爾是則周家肇

punctuated: 原上天建國立君之意，已定於肇生賢嗣之時。甚矣，天眷有周之隆也！既建國為興王之地，又擇賢為嗣業之君，有周之興，豈偶然哉！是詩說者以為叙大王、大伯、王季之德，以及文王伐密、伐崇之事也。而此章之意，若謂天之眷大王也，不惟建國而得其地，抑且立君而得其人。觀夫岐山之陽，木拔道通，有方興未艾之象，是豈人力所能為哉？乃天作此興王之邦也。地闢民歸，啓周家無窮之業，亦豈人力所可致哉？乃天建此興王之國也。然不徒作之邦而已，又必擇其賢者以當之，俾王業有所繼焉；不徒建其國而已，又必擇其賢者以君之，俾統緒有所承焉。天為有周建國立君之意如此，果何所自哉？盖自初生大伯、王季之時而已定矣。故大伯承大王之志而讓其國，人皆以為天意之所存也，殊不知上天眷命，已定於初生大伯之日，而不在於讓國之時，其讓國也，特以成天意爾；王季受大伯之讓而篤其慶，人皆以為天心之所在也，殊不知天命降監，已定於篤生王季之初，而非肇於受讓之際，其受讓也，特以順天心爾。是則周家肇…
translation_en: Tracing the intent of Heaven on high in founding the state and establishing its ruler, we see that it was already determined at the time when the worthy heirs were first born. Profound indeed was Heaven's favor toward the House of Zhou! Having founded the state as the place where true kingship would arise, it further chose a worthy man to be the ruler who would succeed to the enterprise. How could the rise of the House of Zhou have been mere coincidence? Commentators on this ode hold that it recounts the virtues of King Tai, Taibo, and Wang Ji, down to King Wen's expeditions against Mi and Chong. The meaning of this stanza is as if to say that in favoring King Tai, Heaven not only founded the state so that he obtained the right territory, but also established the ruler so that he obtained the right man. Observe how on the southern slopes of Mount Qi, the trees were cleared and paths opened up, displaying signs of a vigor just beginning to flourish and far from subsiding—how could this have been accomplished by human strength? Rather, it was Heaven that created this domain where true kingship would arise. When the land was opened up and the people submitted to him, inaugurating the boundless enterprise of the House of Zhou—how could this, too, have been brought about by human strength? Rather, it was Heaven that founded this state where true kingship would arise. Yet Heaven did not merely create the domain; it also必ず chose a worthy man to match it, so that the royal enterprise might have someone to continue it. It did not merely found the state; it also necessarily chose a worthy man to rule over it, so that the line of succession might have someone to carry it on. Such being Heaven's intent in founding the state and establishing a ruler for the House of Zhou, when did it truly originate? Indeed, it was already determined from the time when Taibo and Wang Ji were first born. Therefore, when Taibo carried out the wishes of King Tai and yielded the state, everyone supposed that Heaven's will lay in that act; they did not realize that the favored mandate of Heaven on high was already determined on the day Taibo was first born, and did not lie in the moment he yielded the state—his yielding the state was merely to fulfill Heaven's will. When Wang Ji accepted Taibo's yielding and consolidated its blessings, everyone supposed that the mind of Heaven resided in that act; they did not realize that Heaven's mandate, looking down from on high, was already determined at the very beginning when Wang Ji was given birth, and did not originate at the juncture when he accepted the yielding—his accepting the yielding was merely to accord with the mind of Heaven. Thus, that the House of Zhou was first…

title: 景泰五年會試錄

translation_en:
… its founding in earlier times and its great succession in later generations were all predetermined by the Mandate of Heaven; how could it have been the work of a single morning or a single evening? Even so, ruling the state and succeeding to the patrimony were the affairs of King Ji; why, then, did the poet speak of Taibo alongside him? Because without Taibo's yielding, there would have been no way to accomplish King Ji's enterprise of building the Zhou; and without King Ji's worthiness, there would have been no way to manifest the glory of Taibo's virtue in yielding. When the poet mentioned them together, was it not indeed fitting?

Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu)

Comment by Associate Examiner Admonisher (Zanshan) Qian 錢: This essay establishes its thesis upon the achievements of the霸 (hegemon) and the transformative influence of the Sage. Its argumentation is rigorous and omits nothing from the commentaries and annotations; its flow of diction is vast yet conforms to the standard rules. It may truly be called the work of one who knows this Classic by heart and gives it expression in words. It should be recorded as a model for scholars.

title: 景泰五年會試錄
text:
考試官洗馬李批此題以齊桓勤怠聖人用
舎為主意諸作雖或得之無所發明獨
此本於傳註諸説立論而文詞蔚然非
熟於是經者不能也
考試官學士商批伯心勤怠聖人用舎實有
關於世道此篇議論正大至謂管仲雖
存無救於桓之衰亦善責備
功有盛衰由伯主有勤怠之異政有得失由聖人有
用舎之殊此齊桓伯功一盛而即衰聖人神化一行
===
而遂沮春秋所以備書而致意焉何則伯者之盛莫
盛于齊桓當周室既衰而所賴以維持世道者寧不
有望於伯主耶幸而齊桓剏伯獨任管仲經營圖回
勤勤不已于幽講盟同尊周室使天下油然興水木
本源之心葵丘束牲大明五禁俾列國昭然守文武
成康之法言歸于好咸諭其志桓於斯時孔子稱其
一匡天下亦已盛矣使由此一轉而王道奚遠哉奈
何伯功方盛君臣俱驕震矜一萌而舉動即異牡丘
之盟謀救徐也八國咸在而救徐之心不協于淮之

考試官學士商批：伯心勤怠、聖人用舎，實有關於世道。此篇議論正大，至謂管仲雖存，無救於桓之衰，亦善責備。

功有盛衰，由伯主有勤怠之異；政有得失，由聖人有用舎之殊。此齊桓伯功一盛而即衰，聖人神化一行而遂沮，《春秋》所以備書而致意焉。何則？伯者之盛，莫盛于齊桓。當周室既衰，而所賴以維持世道者，寧不有望於伯主耶？幸而齊桓剏伯，獨任管仲，經營圖回，勤勤不已。于幽講盟，同尊周室，使天下油然興水木本源之心；葵丘束牲，大明五禁，俾列國昭然守文、武、成、康之法，「言歸于好」，咸諭其志。桓於斯時，孔子稱其一匡天下，亦已盛矣。使由此一轉，而王道奚遠哉？奈何伯功方盛，君臣俱驕，震矜一萌，而舉動即異。牡丘之盟，謀救徐也，八國咸在，而救徐之心不協；于淮之…

Comment by Examiner Li, Librarian (Xianma): The main idea of this topic lies in the diligence and laxity of Duke Huan of Qi, and the employment and dismissal of the Sage. Although other essays sometimes grasped this, they offered no further elucidation. This piece alone bases its argument on the various explanations in the commentaries and annotations, and its literary expression is lush and refined; no one who is not thoroughly versed in this Classic could have written it.

Comment by Examiner Shang, Academician (Xueshi): The diligence and laxity of a hegemon's mind and the employment and dismissal of a sage truly bear upon the state of the world. The argumentation of this essay is upright and grand; where it goes so far as to say that even if Guan Zhong had still been alive, he could not have saved Duke Huan from decline, it also demands perfection well.

That achievements flourish or decline stems from the difference between a hegemon's diligence and laxity; that governance succeeds or fails stems from the distinction between a sage's being employed or set aside. Thus the hegemonic achievement of Duke Huan of Qi no sooner flourished than it declined, and the marvellous transformative influence of the Sage no sooner went into effect than it was blocked—which is why the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) recorded these events in full to convey its deeper meaning. Why is this so? Among the hegemons at their height, none was more flourishing than Duke Huan of Qi. When the House of Zhou had already declined, for that upon which the world relied to uphold moral order, how could one not place hope in a hegemonic lord? Fortunately, Duke Huan of Qi founded the hegemony, entrusting state affairs solely to Guan Zhong, planning and managing with unceasing diligence. At You they held covenants, jointly honoring the House of Zhou, causing the realm spontaneously to arouse sentiments of remembering the source of water and the root of trees; at Kuiqiu they bound the sacrificial victim without slaughtering it and grandly proclaimed the five prohibitions, causing the various states clearly to observe the laws of Kings Wen, Wu, Cheng, and Kang, declaring a "return to amity" as all understood his intent. Of Duke Huan at this time, Confucius praised his uniting and rectifying all under Heaven—it was indeed magnificent! Had he turned from this path toward the Kingly Way, how far off would it have been? Yet how regrettable that just when his hegemonic achievement was at its height, both ruler and minister grew arrogant; once boastful pride sprouted, his actions immediately changed. The covenant at Muqiu was a plan to rescue Xu, yet though eight states were all present, their minds were not united in rescuing Xu; the meeting at the Huai…

title: 景泰五年會試錄
text:
會謀城𨞬也役人夜呼而城𨞬之功不果齊伯至此
衰亦甚焉噫一念勤則功以盛一念怠則功以衰伯
心之有關於世道也如此若夫聖人之盛莫盛于夫
子當魯政陵夷而所賴以興起公室者寧不深望於
聖人耶幸而定公當國克用聖人行乎季孫三月不
違始墮郈邑而叔氏向化則郈不復為公室之斧斤
繼墮費邑而季氏向化則費不復為私家之保障家
不藏甲邑無百雉魯於是時孔子自謂期月而可
亦已驗矣使由此一變而之道奚難哉夫何聖化方
===
行女樂遽受聖轍汶上而政事即乖築蛇淵囿育禽
獸也欲心一縱而已溺游觀之樂大蒐比蒲簡車徒
也侈心一放而不知荒亡之憂魯政至此失亦甚焉
噫人存則其政舉人亡則其政息聖人之有益於人
國也又如此雖然說者謂桓公伯衰管仲之既亡□
聖人化沮季孫之專魯也愚謂季孫之沮聖化誠然

translation_en:
… meeting at Huai was to plan the walling of Zeng; the laborers cried out in the night, and the work of walling Zeng came to nothing. By this point, the hegemony of Qi had declined severely indeed. Alas! With a single thought of diligence, achievements flourish; with a single thought of indolence, achievements decline. Such is the bearing of a hegemon's mind upon the way of the world.

As for the flourishing of a sage, none surpassed the Master [Confucius]. When the governance of Lu had fallen into decay, how could those who looked for the revival of the ducal house not place their deepest hopes in the sage? Fortunately, when Duke Ding held the reins of the state, he was able to employ the sage, acting through Ji Sun, and for three months there was no违 [deviation from his counsel]. First, the town of Hou was dismantled, and the Shusun clan turned toward his transforming influence, so that Hou no longer served as an axe against the ducal house; next, the town of Bi was dismantled, and the Jisun clan turned toward his transforming influence, so that Bi no longer served as a stronghold for a private family. Noble families did not hoard armor, and no town had walls of a hundred *zhi*. In Lu at that time, what Confucius himself meant by saying "in the course of a year, much could be done" had already been borne out. Had Lu undergone one transformation from this point, how would reaching the true Way have been difficult?

Yet why was it that just as the sage's transforming influence was taking effect, the female musicians were suddenly accepted? The sage's carriage tracks turned toward the Wen River, and affairs of government immediately went awry. Constructing the park at Sheyuan was for breeding birds and beasts; once the mind of desire was indulged, the ruler was already drowned in the pleasures of sightseeing and excursion. Holding the great military review at Bipu was for inspecting chariots and foot soldiers; once the mind of extravagance was let loose, he knew nothing of the perils of dissipation and ruin. By this point, the governance of Lu had gone grievously astray. Alas! When the right men are present, governance is upheld; when those men are gone, governance ceases. Such, again, is the benefit a sage brings to a state.

Even so, commentators say that the decline of Duke Huan's hegemony was because Guan Zhong had already died [?], and that the obstruction of the sage's transforming influence was due to Ji Sun's monopolization of Lu. In my humble view, that Ji Sun obstructed the sage's transformation is certainly true; yet to say that as long as Guan Zhong was present the hegemony of Qi did not decline is, I fear, not so. From the time Duke Huan entered the state in the ninth year of Duke Zhuang until the campaign at Kuiqiu was more than thirty years, whereas earlier Confucians said that he solely entrusted state affairs to Guan Zhong for over forty years—which means that this was while Guan Zhong was still alive. Now, Guan Zhong was never originally a talent fit to assist a true king…

title: 景泰五年會試錄
text:
當况文有發揮必熟於春秋者
春秋因使命而予大夫用義之專復因使命而予大
夫守禮之正此可見高子屈完奉君非義而能制之
以義寗俞昭子遇人非禮而能却之以禮春秋得不
均予之哉嗟夫禮義人之大閑也當春秋之世而能
以禮義自處者誰耶今而魯有內難齊桓是圖使高
子將兵以為窺魯之計齊師次陘楚人震恐使屈完
如師而為覘齊之行其命之非其義矣使二子不明
此而將順之豈事君之義耶唯高子至則以平難善
===
鄰而不從其兼國廣地之念屈完至則以服義遷善
而不行其負固不服之心一則保人宗社於既危一
則全巳人民於不戰雖違其君之命而不之計然惟
義所在而必從焉所謂出境有可以安國家利社稷
則專之可也春秋所以於二子皆不稱使非予其用
義之專乎若夫衛成復國使俞脩好而魯也享之以
彤弓湛露之詩魯昭被訴使婼往謝而晋也加之以
邾夷共坐之辱其待之非其禮矣使二子不察此而
□受之豈守身之禮耶惟寗俞聞歌則知天子之詩

punctuated:
當，况文有發揮，必熟於《春秋》者。

《春秋》因使命而予大夫用義之專，復因使命而予大夫守禮之正。此可見高子、屈完奉君非義，而能制之以義；寗俞、昭子遇人非禮，而能却之以禮。《春秋》得不均予之哉？嗟夫！禮義，人之大閑也。當春秋之世，而能以禮義自處者誰耶？今而魯有內難，齊桓是圖，使高子將兵，以為窺魯之計；齊師次陘，楚人震恐，使屈完如師，而為覘齊之行。其命之非其義矣。使二子不明此而將順之，豈事君之義耶？唯高子至，則以平難善鄰，而不從其兼國廣地之念；屈完至，則以服義遷善，而不行其負固不服之心。一則保人宗社於既危，一則全巳人民於不戰。雖違其君之命而不之計，然惟義所在而必從焉，所謂「出境有可以安國家、利社稷，則專之可也」。《春秋》所以於二子皆不稱「使」，非予其用義之專乎？若夫衛成復國，使俞脩好，而魯也享之以《彤弓》、《湛露》之詩；魯昭被訴，使婼往謝，而晋也加之以邾夷共坐之辱。其待之非其禮矣。使二子不察此而□受之，豈守身之禮耶？惟寗俞聞歌，則知天子之詩，
translation_en:
…apt. Moreover, the essay displays real elaboration; its author must be thoroughly versed in the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu).

On account of diplomatic missions, the Spring and Autumn Annals commends grandees for exercising independent discretion in accordance with righteousness, and again on account of diplomatic missions, it commends grandees for upholding the rectitude of ritual propriety. From this we can see that Master Gao (Gaozi 高子) and Qu Wan 屈完 received unrighteous commands from their rulers yet were able to regulate them through righteousness, while Ning Yu 寗俞 and Master Zhao (Shusun Zhaozi 叔孫昭子, i.e., Shusun婼) encountered treatment from others that violated ritual propriety yet were able to repulse it through ritual propriety. Could the Spring and Autumn Annals fail to commend them equally? Alas! Ritual propriety and righteousness are the great bounds of human conduct. In the age of the Spring and Autumn period, who was able to conduct himself according to ritual propriety and righteousness? Now, when Lu 魯 suffered internal disorder, Duke Huan of Qi 齊桓公 harbored designs against it and sent Master Gao to lead troops as a scheme to spy out Lu; when the army of Qi halted at Xing 陘, the men of Chu 楚 were terrified and sent Qu Wan to go to the army on a mission to reconnoiter Qi. The commands given to them were unrighteous. Had the two masters failed to understand this and simply complied with them, how would that have been the righteousness of serving one's ruler? Only when Master Gao arrived did he act to pacify the disorder and maintain good neighborly relations, refusing to follow his ruler's desire to annex a state and expand his territory; and when Qu Wan arrived, he acted to submit to righteousness and move toward the good, refusing to carry out his ruler's intention of relying on natural strongholds and remaining recalcitrant. The one preserved another's ancestral temples and altars of the soil and grain when they were already in peril; the other kept his own people whole without resorting to war. Although they disobeyed their rulers' commands without regard for the consequences, wherever righteousness lay they unfailingly followed it—this is what is meant by the saying, "Once across the border, if there is something by which one can bring peace to the state and benefit the altars of the soil and grain, it is permissible to act on one's own authority." Thus, the reason the Spring and Autumn Annals does not refer to either of the two masters as an "envoy" (shi 使)—is it not to commend them for exercising independent discretion in accordance with righteousness? As for Duke Cheng of Wei 衛成公 being restored to his state and sending Ning Yu to renew friendly relations, Lu feasted him with the odes "Red Bow" (Tonggong 彤弓) and "Heavy Dew" (Zhanlu 湛露); and when Duke Zhao of Lu 魯昭公 was accused, he sent Shusun Chuo 叔孫婼 to go and apologize, whereupon Jin 晋 subjected him to the humiliation of sitting together with the barbarian of Zhu 邾. The way they were treated violated ritual propriety. Had the two masters failed to discern this and [passively?] accepted it, how would that have been the ritual propriety of preserving one's personal integrity? Only when Ning Yu heard the singing did he recognize that they were odes belonging to the Son of Heaven…

肯出貨以苟容一則辭人尊己而不褻一則却人辱
己而不屈雖違其國之命而不之恤然惟禮所在而

年而內大夫之賢惟一叔孫焉則人才已不如春秋

而不敢干禮以取戾；叔孫遭變，則執先王之制而不肯出貨以苟容。一則辭人尊己而不褻，一則却人辱己而不屈，雖違其國之命而不之恤，然惟禮所在而必守焉，可謂「使於四方，能專對而不辱命」者矣。《春秋》所以於二子或書名、或書氏，又非予其守禮之正乎？雖然，賢如四子，在春秋衰世，宜不多得，可足嘉已。然自閔而至于文四十年間，而外大夫之賢者三見焉，則春秋之初猶多士也；自文而下至於昭公百有餘年，而內大夫之賢惟一叔孫焉，則人才已不如春秋之初矣，又况意如專魯，徒有其賢而不盡其用也。噫！

「凡侍於君，紳垂，足如履齊，頤霤，垂拱，視下而聽上，視帶以及袷，聽鄉任左。」
趙歅

…and did not dare transgress the rites and thereby incur blame; when Shusun 叔孫 encountered a crisis, he held fast to the institutions of the former kings and refused to offer bribes merely to gain easy accommodation. The one declined others' exaltation of himself and was not presumptuous; the other repelled others' humiliation of himself and did not yield. Even if they departed from the commands of their states without concern, they steadfastly upheld whatever the rites required; they may truly be called men who, "sent to the four quarters, are able to reply on their own initiative and not disgrace their commission." Is not the reason the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) sometimes records the personal name and sometimes the clan name of these two men likewise to praise the rectitude with which they upheld the rites? Even so, worthies such as these four men were naturally hard to find in the declining age of the Spring and Autumn period, and are well worthy of commendation. Yet in the forty years from Duke Min 閔公 to Duke Wen 文公, worthy grand masters from outside states appear three times, showing that at the beginning of the Spring and Autumn period there were still many capable men. From Duke Wen down to Duke Zhao 昭公, over a span of more than a hundred years, among the grand masters within Lu 魯 there was only a single worthy, Shusun; thus talent was already no match for what it had been at the beginning of the Spring and Autumn period—how much more so when Yiru 意如 (Ji Pingzi 季平子) monopolized power in Lu, so that even though it possessed his worthiness, he could not be employed to the fullest! Alas!

Record of Rites (Liji)
"Whenever one attends upon the ruler, the sash hangs down, the feet are as if treading on the hem of the robe, the chin inclines like eaves, the hands are clasped and hanging low; one looks downward and listens upward, looking between the girdle and the collar, and turning the ear toward the left."
Zhao Yin 趙歅

title: 景泰五年會試錄
text:
臣侍君之禮不泛不畧結引聖人為法
尤髙非潜心於禮者不能也宜在所取
考試官洗馬李批人臣侍君容節敬為之
本也此作盖得其旨矣
考試官學士商批此篇以敬立說文無浮
詞可取
人臣之侍於君其儀容視聽一於敬而已夫敬者人
臣事君之本也苟侍於君側而儀容視聽有不敬焉
豈足以盡事君之道哉今夫臣之於君尊卑有定分
===
===
上下有定禮而敬可以少懈乎故凡侍於君也立焉
而拱則身如磬折大帶下垂而立容辯也身折則裳
齊委地足如履齊而足容重也頭容固欲其直侍於
君側其身俯故頭容臨前而頥之垂如屋霤然手容
固欲其恭侍於君側其容屈故手之拱者亦下垂焉
豈故為是足恭哉敬之著於儀容者然也儀容既極
其敬而見於視聽者又可以少忽乎是故視雖在下
而必側面向上以聽君之言則與髙目下耳以尊臨
卑者不同視而髙不過祫卑不下帶則與上於面則
