… the rites of a minister attending upon his ruler, being neither vague nor sketchy; the conclusion citing the Sage as a model is especially lofty. None who had not immersed his mind in the rites could have produced this; it rightly deserves to be selected.

Examiner Li, Librarian of the Supervisorate of Imperial Instruction, comments: In the demeanor and comportment of a minister attending upon his ruler, reverence is the foundation. This composition has indeed grasped the essential meaning.

Examiner Shang, Hanlin Academician, comments: This essay establishes its argument on the basis of reverence, and the writing contains no empty verbiage. It is worthy of selection.

When a minister attends upon his ruler, his demeanor, gaze, and listening are unified solely in reverence. Now reverence is the foundation of a minister's service to his ruler. If, when attending at the ruler's side, there is any lack of reverence in his demeanor, gaze, or listening, how could that suffice to fulfill the way of serving a ruler? Now between a minister and his ruler, noble and humble have fixed stations, superior and inferior have fixed rites—how then could reverence be relaxed even slightly? Therefore, whenever one attends upon the ruler: as one stands with hands clasped, the body bends like a musical stone, the great sash hangs down, and one's standing posture is humble and deferential; because the body bends, the hem of the lower garment trails on the ground, the feet seem to tread upon the hem, and the bearing of the feet is grave; the carriage of the head ordinarily ought to be upright, yet in attending at the ruler's side one's body stoops, so the head inclines forward and the chin hangs down like the eaves of a roof; the carriage of the hands ordinarily ought to be respectful, yet in attending at the ruler's side one's posture is bowed, so the clasped hands likewise hang down. Is this done deliberately as excessive servility? Rather, it is how reverence manifests itself in one's demeanor. Once demeanor has reached the utmost reverence, how can what is shown in gazing and listening be neglected even slightly? Therefore, although one's gaze is directed downward, one must turn the face upward from the side to listen to the ruler's words—which differs from looking high and listening low when a superior looks down upon an inferior. In gazing, one looks no higher than the collar and no lower than the sash—which differs from looking above the face, which…

text:
傲下於帶則憂者有異立者尊右坐者尊左侍而君
坐則臣在君之右故聽鄉皆任左以向君焉又豈故
為是諂媚哉敬之寓於視聽者然也雖然此特記人
臣侍君之禮爾觀夫孔子之入公門則鞠躬如也過
位則色勃如也出則逞顏色怡怡如也没階趨翼如
也則聖人事君於出入進退之際無適不極其敬豈
獨侍於君側為然哉噫聖人事君盡禮如此彼以為
諂者惡足與言禮
君子以此之為尊敬然然後以其所能教百姓

translation_en:
…arrogant, and lower than the sash appears忧 [sorrowful]. For those who stand, the right side is honored; for those who sit, the left side is honored. When attending a ruler who is seated, the subject stands to the ruler's right; therefore, in listening and facing, he inclines his left side toward the ruler. Why would he deliberately act so flatteringly? It is simply how reverence is lodged in looking and listening. Even so, this merely records the ritual of a subject attending his ruler. Observe how Confucius, upon entering the duke's gate, bowed his body respectfully; when passing the empty throne, his countenance changed suddenly; when coming out and descending the first step, his expression relaxed and became pleased and genial; and at the bottom of the steps, he glided forward as though with outstretched wings. Thus, when the Sage served his ruler, in every moment of entering, exiting, advancing, and withdrawing, there was nowhere he did not carry his reverence to the utmost—how could this be true only when attending at the ruler's side? Alas! The Sage served his ruler with such complete ritual propriety; how could those who considered it flattery be worthy of discussing ritual!

"The superior man regards these as worthy of honor and reverence; and only then does he teach the common people with what he is capable of, not neglecting their common seasons and degrees. Only when there is accomplished achievement does he fashion carvings, emblems, and embroidered ceremonial robes to pass them down."
Zhao Xin 趙歆

Examiner and Librarian of the Left Secretariat of the Heir Apparent Li commented: Taking the establishment of teachings to guide the people and the adornment of objects to transmit them afar as the substance of valuing rites accords with the original meaning of the text; it is worthy of selection.

Examiner and Academician Shang commented: It brings out the meaning of why the noble man honors rites, deeply fitting the assigned topic.

In the noble man's high regard for the great rites, he on the one hand relies on the people's capabilities to establish teachings suited to the times, and on the other hand relies on ritual occasions to adorn objects so as to transmit them afar. Now, the function of rites is great indeed, and it is what the noble man ought to value. Yet without establishing teachings to guide the people and adorning objects to transmit them afar, how else could one see the actual substance of valuing rites?

In the past, when the Master replied to Duke Ai's question, "Why does the noble man speak of rites with such reverence?", he held that rites are the regulations and refinements of heavenly principle and the ceremonial standards of human affairs. In the unseen realm, in reverently serving the great spirits, without rites there is no way to regulate it; in the visible realm, in distinguishing the great human relationships, without rites there is no way to order them. Since the function of rites is such as this, how could the noble man not exalt and revere them with solemn respect to show the weight he attaches to them?

And how could he merely attach weight to them? He must also rely on what the people are capable of doing in order to establish his teachings. For rites are rooted in the heavenly order; things such as the constant norms of human relationships in daily life are all what the people are capable of practicing. The noble man relies on what they are capable of practicing and formulates regulations and refinements for them; therefore, there must be set times for performing the rites. Thus, capping and marriage have the appointed times for capping and marriage, and burial and sacrifice have the appointed times for burial and sacrifice. When the appointed times and seasons are constant, the people will all follow them without transgression and abide by them without neglect.

Such is the way teachings are rooted in rites; and how is it that rites are transmitted afar? Therefore, days may be distant or near, and one must…

宗廟敬祭祀以見君子之嚴於事神醜衣服卑宮室
至於與民同利以見君子之儉於奉己然則古之君
子周於禮也如此舉而措之國寧有不治乎惜乎哀

龜從筮從，而後事可成也。君子諏日云吉，而敬以將事，又必飾物以存禮焉。於是治其雕刻鏤畫之文，以為祭器之飾；施其文章黼黻之美，以為祭服之飾。器服恒存，則禮可因之而不泯，續之於無窮矣。君子重禮之實，至是殆無以加矣。吾夫子舉以為哀公告，其旨不亦深哉！不特此也，下文又告以備鼎俎、設豕腊、脩宗廟、敬祭祀，以見君子之嚴於事神；醜衣服、卑宮室，至於與民同利，以見君子之儉於奉已。然則古之君子周於禮也如此，舉而措之，國寧有不治乎？惜乎哀公徒問而不能行也。

translation_en:
… tortoise shell and yarrow stalks both concur before the matter can be accomplished. Once the superior man consults about the day and finds it auspicious, he conducts the affair with reverence, and he must also adorn ritual objects in order to preserve the rites. Accordingly, he fashions patterns of carving, engraving, and painting as ornaments for sacrificial vessels, and applies the beauty of colorful emblems and ceremonial motifs as ornaments for sacrificial vestments. When vessels and vestments are permanently preserved, the rites can rely upon them so as not to perish, continuing into the boundless future. The reality of the superior man's esteem for the rites could hardly be surpassed at this point. When our Master cited this to inform Duke Ai (Ai Gong 哀公), how profound was his meaning! Nor is this all. In the following passage he further informed him of preparing tripods and meat-stands, setting out dried pork, repairing the ancestral temples, and revering the sacrifices, so as to show the superior man's solemnity in serving the spirits; and of wearing coarse clothing and dwelling in humble palaces, to the point of sharing benefits with the common people, so as to show the superior man's frugality in maintaining himself. Since the superior men of antiquity were so comprehensive in the rites, if one were to take these up and put them into practice, how could a state fail to be well governed? Alas, Duke Ai merely asked about them and was unable to carry them out.

text:
理得非他卷可比也
考試官學士商批論有議論有抑揚與場
中只作四書義者不侔矣
大矣哉聖人之善也不私於一己而公於天下焉夫
莫大於天下之善尤莫大於聖人公天下之善聖人公
天下之善以為善則天下之善皆聖人之善矣此舜
之善與人同所以為聖之至也歟嗟夫天之賦於人
者無異也天地之塞吾其體天地之帥吾其性性之
同者同此至善之理也何獨聖人能公其善於天下
===
耶誠以世之人均禀此善而能知善之為善者鮮焉
自是者不知不足在己雖己未善也未必能舍以從
人自用者不知有餘在人雖人有善也未必能取之
於己私之身者隔形骸而梏爾汝私之家者隔門墻
而分彼此孰知所謂公天下之善哉惟舜之心廣大
光明萬理畢具一有感觸其應甚速是以己有未善
無一毫係吝而舍之以從人不啻如春融氷釋渾渾
然無形迹也人或有善無一毫勉强而樂取之於己
不啻如巨海納流浩浩然無涯涘也當其耕稼陶漁

自是者不知不足在已雖已未善也未必能舍以從

於已私之身者隔形骸而梏爾汝私之家者隔門墻
而分彼此孰知所謂公天下之善哉惟舜之心廣大
光明萬理畢具一有感觸其應甚速是以已有未善
無一毫係吝而舍之以從人不啻如春融氷釋渾渾
然無形迹也人或有善無一毫勉強而樂取之於已
不啻如巨海納流浩浩然無涯涘也當其耕稼陶漁
punctuated:
理得，非他卷可比也。
考試官學士商批：論有議論，有抑揚，與場中只作四書義者不侔矣。
大矣哉，聖人之善也！不私於一己，而公於天下焉。夫莫大於天下之善，尤莫大於聖人公天下之善。聖人公天下之善以為善，則天下之善皆聖人之善矣。此舜之善與人同，所以為聖之至也歟！嗟夫！天之賦於人者無異也。天地之塞，吾其體；天地之帥，吾其性。性之同者，同此至善之理也。何獨聖人能公其善於天下耶？誠以世之人均禀此善，而能知善之為善者鮮焉。自是者不知不足在己，雖己未善也，未必能舍以從人；自用者不知有餘在人，雖人有善也，未必能取之於己。私之身者，隔形骸而梏爾汝；私之家者，隔門墻而分彼此。孰知所謂公天下之善哉！惟舜之心廣大光明，萬理畢具，一有感觸，其應甚速。是以己有未善，無一毫係吝，而舍之以從人，不啻如春融氷釋，渾渾然無形迹也；人或有善，無一毫勉强，而樂取之於己，不啻如巨海納流，浩浩然無涯涘也。當其耕稼陶漁
translation_en:
… and the principles are grasped; it cannot be compared with other papers.

Examiner and Academician Shang [Lu 商輅] comments: The discourse contains real argumentation and has cadence and modulation; it is not on a par with those in the examination compound who merely write in the style of Four Books expositions.

Great indeed is the goodness of the sage! He does not keep it selfishly for himself alone, but shares it publicly with all under Heaven. Now, nothing is greater than the goodness of all under Heaven, and even more, nothing is greater than the sage making the goodness of all under Heaven public. When the sage takes the shared goodness of all under Heaven as his own goodness, then all the goodness in the world becomes the sage's goodness. Is this not why Shun's holding goodness in common with others makes him the ultimate sage?

Alas! What Heaven endows in human beings is no different. That which fills Heaven and Earth is my body; that which directs Heaven and Earth is my nature. Where human nature is the same, it shares this same principle of supreme goodness. Why is it that the sage alone can make his goodness public throughout the world? Truly it is because although the people of the world are all equally endowed with this goodness, few are able to recognize that goodness is truly good. Those who consider themselves right do not know that deficiency lies within themselves; even when they themselves are not yet good, they are not necessarily able to set themselves aside to follow others. Those who rely only on themselves do not know that abundance lies in others; even when others possess goodness, they are not necessarily able to adopt it for themselves. Those who are selfish with regard to their own persons divide physical forms and fetter themselves with "you" and "I"; those who are selfish with regard to their families divide gates and walls and distinguish "that" from "this." Who among them understands what is meant by making the goodness of all under Heaven public?

Only the mind of Shun was vast, great, and luminous, complete with all principles; as soon as it was stirred, its response was exceedingly swift. Therefore, when there was anything not yet good in himself, without the slightest attachment or grudging he set it aside to follow others—just like ice melting in the warmth of spring, seamlessly leaving no trace behind. And when others happened to possess some goodness, without the slightest forcing he gladly adopted it as his own—just like the vast sea receiving flowing streams, boundlessly without shore or limit. In the days when he plowed, sowed, made pottery, and fished…

而舜之處此則稽于衆之心不少替焉及其登庸在

取善不異于後日夫舜之取善非己之善真有所不
足也其不足者惟日不足之心耳觀其内之治必咨
於九官九官豈賢於舜哉然而咨九官者取九官之
善也九官之善即大舜之善也觀其外之治必命十

其善也而十二牧之善即大舜之善也又如命禹徂
征三苗而負固不服三苗適自取罪爾於舜何損焉
舜則聞伯益之德言聽大禹之班師誕敷文德而置

為在人矣其公天下之善如此誰其及之子路聞過

punctuated: 之日，人但見與木石居、與鹿豕遊，若無與天下之善；而舜之處此，則稽于衆之心不少替焉。及其登庸在位之日，人但知受堯之禪、陟堯之位，若無與天下之善；而舜之處此，則好問好察之心不少間焉。自側微而至四岳，其取善不改於初心；未即位而居攝政，其取善不異于後日。夫舜之取善，非己之善真有所不足也；其不足者，惟日不足之心耳。觀其内之治，必咨於九官。九官豈賢於舜哉？然而咨九官者，取九官之善也；九官之善，即大舜之善也。觀其外之治，必命十二牧。十二牧豈復出於舜之右哉？然而命之者，亦取其善也；而十二牧之善，即大舜之善也。又如命禹徂征三苗，而負固不服。三苗適自取罪爾，於舜何損焉？舜則聞伯益之德言，聽大禹之班師，誕敷文德，而置三苗於度外，其汲汲於舍己之未善而從人之善，何如哉！是知舜以一人之善而合天下之善，合天下之善而為一己之善，善與人同，而亦不知孰為在己、孰為在人矣。其公天下之善如此，誰其及之？子路聞過則喜，異乎常人矣，而猶待有過而後樂聞之也，固不
translation_en: … days [when he farmed, made pottery, and fished], people only saw him dwelling with trees and rocks and roaming with deer and swine, as though he had nothing to do with the goodness of the world; yet in this situation, Shun's mind of consulting the multitude never slackened in the least. When it came to the days when he was elevated and employed on the throne, people only knew that he received Yao's abdication and ascended Yao's throne, as though he had nothing to do with the goodness of the world; yet in this situation, Shun's mind of loving to question and loving to examine shallow words never ceased for a moment. From his humble obscurity to his recommendation by the Four Peaks, his adoption of goodness did not change from his original intention; before he ascended the throne, while serving as regent, his adoption of goodness did not differ from that of his later days. Now, Shun's adopting goodness was not because his own goodness was truly deficient in any way; what was deficient was simply a mind that felt the day was never long enough. Look at his governance of the interior: he invariably consulted the Nine Officials. Were the Nine Officials worthier than Shun? Yet in consulting the Nine Officials, he adopted the goodness of the Nine Officials; the goodness of the Nine Officials thus became the goodness of Great Shun. Look at his governance of the exterior: he invariably charged the Twelve Pastors. Did the Twelve Pastors surpass Shun? Yet in charging them, he likewise adopted their goodness; and the goodness of the Twelve Pastors thus became the goodness of Great Shun. Take again the instance when he commanded Yu to go and punish the Three Miao, who relied on their strongholds and refused to submit. The Three Miao were merely bringing guilt upon themselves—what loss was that to Shun? Yet Shun heeded Boyi's words on virtue, listened to Great Yu's withdrawal of the troops, widely diffused civil virtue, and put the Three Miao out of his calculations. How eager he was to set aside what was not yet good in himself and follow the goodness of others! From this we know that Shun united the goodness of the whole world with the goodness of a single man, and made the goodness of the whole world his own personal goodness; sharing goodness with others, he no longer knew which belonged to himself and which belonged to others. Making the goodness of the world common to all like this—who could ever match him? That Zilu rejoiced whenever he heard of his faults made him different from ordinary men, yet he still had to wait until he had a fault before he gladly heard of it; certainly that was not…

…equal the great Shun in making goodness public to all. The great Yu bowed whenever he heard good words, which set him above Zilu, yet even he was not entirely free of conscious effort—how could that compare with Shun's making goodness public wholly out of natural spontaneity? Moreover, when one adopts the goodness of others, those who are good are all the more encouraged to do good; thus one also helps them in their doing of good. Alas! Beginning by adopting the goodness of others to make it one's own goodness, and ending by using one's own goodness to help others do good—since Shun's time, who has succeeded him in this? Fortunately today there is a Sage on the throne above.

translation_en:
…the weal and woe [of the people]; whether one employs the worthy or employs flatterers bears upon the security or peril of the altars of soil and grain. Antiquity had admonitory rules, which today ought to serve as our standard.

Now, I humbly encounter [His Majesty the Emperor]: endowed by Heaven with a dragon-like bearing, his sage virtue daily renewed; heeding remonstrance like a flowing stream, having long personally practiced benevolence and righteousness; seeking the worthy as if athirst, hoping for assistance in bringing about Great Peace. Indeed, in sageness you rival the Lord of Yu [Shun]—what need is there to wait until hearing Boyi to cultivate virtue? Yet in my rashness I resemble Jia Yi, who nonetheless wished to offer loyalty on behalf of Emperor Wen. Thus I have composed the "Admonition on the Great Treasure" (Dabao zhi zhen), venturing to importune the imperial hearing.

At the outset it recites the purport that "to be a ruler is truly difficult," and in the middle it strictly warns against theincipient tendency of indulging desires to the ruin of moral norms. When the eight delicacies are arrayed before one, there is the fear of reaching the point of mounds of dregs and pools of wine; to make majestic the ninefold palace within, what need is there for chambers of jasper and terraces of jade? Reverently match the prudent care of King Wen of Zhou; expansively embody the magnanimity of Emperor Gaozu of Han. If you wish to secure your position, it lies in taking this admonition as a mirror.

Without measuring my own humble woodgatherer's words, I brashly risk the executioner's axe to sully Your Majesty's perusal, hoping it may penetrate the depths of your heart. Meeting the eye and alerting the mind, may caution and apprehension abide alone in utmost stillness; embodied within and manifested without, may order and peace truly be preserved without end. I respectfully take the "[Admonition on the] Great…" that I have set forth…

punctuated: 當代之制作，所以革舊俗之弊而追蹤千古。孟子曰：「先聖後聖，其揆一也。」夫豈有異乎哉？昔者龍馬負圖而出於河，伏羲因之而畫八卦：乾、坎、艮、震、巽、離、坤、兌，而吉凶、存亡、進退之道著焉，所以教民趨吉而避凶也。神龜負書而出於洛，大禹因之而叙九疇：五行、五事、八政、五紀、皇極、三德、稽疑、庶徵、福極，而民生日用彝倫之道備焉，所以訓民為善而去惡也。羲、禹二聖之制作，其繼天立極而垂憲萬世，誠卓卓乎不可尚已！三代而下，未見有能繼之者。洪惟我太祖高皇帝統一華夷，慮胡習之未除、人心之未淑，條成《大誥》三編，頒布天下。如郭桓貪汙無恥而君臣之道廢，則錄之以示戒；而又有〈君臣同遊〉之章，使天下曉然知君臣之有義。如夢弼私替贓私而父子之道壞，則紀之以示懲；而又有〈明孝〉之章，使天下昭然知父子之有親。無非申明五常，欲民同歸於至善，其與羲、禹垂教之意何殊哉？迨…
translation_en:
…The institutions created in the present dynasty are the means by which the abuses of old customs are reformed and the footsteps of remotest antiquity are followed. Mencius (Mengzi 孟子) said: "The former sages and the latter sages—their principles are one and the same." How could there be any difference between them?

In antiquity, the dragon-horse emerged from the Yellow River bearing the Diagram on its back, and on this basis Fuxi 伏羲 drew the Eight Trigrams—Qian 乾, Kan 坎, Gen 艮, Zhen 震, Xun 巽, Li 離, Kun 坤, and Dui 兌—whereby the principles of good and ill fortune, preservation and ruin, advancing and retreating were made manifest; this was how he taught the people to pursue good fortune and avoid calamity. The divine tortoise emerged from the Luo River bearing the Writing on its shell, and on this basis Great Yu 大禹 set forth in order the Nine Categories—the Five Phases, the Five Conducts, the Eight Administrations, the Five Regulators of Time, the August Ultimate, the Three Virtues, the Examination of Doubts, the Various Verifications, and the Five Blessings and Six Extremities—whereby the principles of the invariable human relationships in the people's daily lives were made complete; this was how he instructed the people to do good and cast off evil. The creations of the two sages Fuxi and Yu, in succeeding Heaven to establish the ultimate standard and handing down laws for ten thousand generations, were truly so eminent that nothing can surpass them! From the Three Dynasties downward, none has been seen who could succeed them.

I reflect with awe on how our Grand Progenitor, Emperor Gao (Taizu Gaohuangdi 太祖高皇帝), unified Chinese and barbarians. Concerned that northern barbarian customs had not yet been eradicated and that human hearts had not yet been made pure, he compiled the Three Compilations of the Grand Pronouncements (Dagao sanbian 大誥三編) in detailed articles and promulgated them throughout the realm. For instance, when Guo Huan 郭桓 was corrupt and shameless, so that the Way of ruler and minister was abandoned, the Emperor recorded his case to serve as a warning; yet there was also the chapter on "Ruler and Ministers Sharing Fellowship" (Junchen tongyou 君臣同遊), causing all under Heaven to understand clearly that between ruler and minister there is righteousness. Likewise, when Mengbi 夢弼 privately substituted illicitly acquired goods [for his father?], so that the Way of father and son was ruined, the Emperor chronicled his case to serve as a deterrent; yet there was also the chapter on "Clarifying Filial Piety" (Mingxiao 明孝), causing all under Heaven to see clearly that between father and son there is affection. All of this was nothing other than reiterating and clarifying the Five Constant Virtues, desiring that the people should together return to the highest good. title: 景泰五年會試錄
text:
呵成亦善荅者
時有聖人而斯道之寄在於人時無聖人而斯
道之寄在於書在於人者將欲以傳道在於書
者惟欲以明道將欲傳道則見於講論者不能
不因乎人何也有聖人為之宗主也將欲明道
則見于著述者不能不致其詳何也無聖人為
之宗主也有聖人為之宗主則雖不言而終則
自明之矣無聖人為之宗主則始或不言而終
則無能明之者矣是則聖人之有所不言非不
===
言也不必言也賢人之有所言非有言也不能
不言也言若背乎聖人而實不異於聖人意若
乖於聖人而實有合於聖人此聖賢憂世憫道
之本心也論語一書說者謂成於曾子門人子
思之徒宜其言之不異也然命之與仁夫子罕
言性與天道不可得聞中庸則備言之者盖論
語恐學者未易曉故聖人不形諸言中庸為傳
道而作故子思不得不備言以示人也子路問
事鬼神而聖人不告中庸則極言鬼神之德之

呵成，亦善荅者。

時有聖人，而斯道之寄在於人；時無聖人，而斯道之寄在於書。在於人者，將欲以傳道；在於書者，惟欲以明道。將欲傳道，則見於講論者，不能不因乎人。何也？有聖人為之宗主也。將欲明道，則見于著述者，不能不致其詳。何也？無聖人為之宗主也。有聖人為之宗主，則雖不言，而終則自明之矣；無聖人為之宗主，則始或不言，而終則無能明之者矣。是則聖人之有所不言，非不言也，不必言也；賢人之有所言，非有言也，不能不言也。言若背乎聖人，而實不異於聖人；意若乖於聖人，而實有合於聖人。此聖賢憂世憫道之本心也。《論語》一書，說者謂成於曾子門人、子思之徒，宜其言之不異也。然命之與仁，夫子罕言；性與天道，不可得聞；《中庸》則備言之者，盖《論語》恐學者未易曉，故聖人不形諸言；《中庸》為傳道而作，故子思不得不備言以示人也。子路問事鬼神，而聖人不告；《中庸》則極言鬼神之德之
translation_en:
…in a single breath; this too is one who answers well.

When the age has a sage, the repository of this Way lies in the person; when the age has no sage, the repository of this Way lies in books. When it lies in the person, the intention is to transmit the Way; when it lies in books, the sole intention is to elucidate the Way. When the intention is to transmit the Way, what appears in discourses and discussions cannot but be tailored to the person. Why is this? Because there is a sage to serve as its presiding master. When the intention is to elucidate the Way, what appears in writings cannot but be set forth in full detail. Why is this? Because there is no sage to serve as its presiding master. When there is a sage to serve as its presiding master, even if he does not speak of something, in the end it will naturally become clear; when there is no sage to serve as its presiding master, if at the outset one does not speak of it, in the end there will be no one able to make it clear. Thus, where the sage left things unsaid, it was not that he would not speak of them, but that he did not need to speak of them; where the worthies spoke of things, it was not that they merely wished to speak, but that they could not help speaking of them. Their words seem to run counter to the sage, yet in reality do not differ from the sage; their meaning seems at odds with the sage, yet in reality accords with the sage. This is the fundamental heart of the sages and worthies in their concern for the world and compassion for the Way. As for the book the Analects (Lunyu), commentators say that it was compiled by the disciples of Zengzi and the followers of Zisi, so it would be fitting that their words should not differ. Yet the Master rarely spoke of destiny and humaneness, and his views on human nature and the Way of Heaven could not be heard, whereas the Doctrine of the Mean (Zhongyong) speaks of them exhaustively. This is because in the Analects, for fear that learners might not easily understand, the sage did not put them into words; whereas the Doctrine of the Mean was written to transmit the Way, and therefore Zisi could not help speaking of them exhaustively to show them to others. Zilu asked about serving ghosts and spirits, and the sage did not tell him, whereas the Doctrine of the Mean speaks to the utmost of how the virtue of ghosts and spirits…

text:
故在聖人恐子路失進學之序子思則欲揭是
經以明夫道之費隐二書之旨何背乎論語謂
宋不足徵傷殷之文獻不足吾從先進設言若
用禮樂則當損過以就中耳而中庸主為下不
倍而言殷禮雖存然非當世之法孔子既不得
位則從時王之制而已論語稱周之至德盖指
文王然伐紂之舉文有可取之勢而不取武非
有心於取而不容不取一聽於天而已一聽於天
則無害於繼志述事矣此中庸所以稱之也二
===
日之言何背乎子思夫子之孫也而中庸直言
仲尼盖古者生無爵死無謚則子孫有名之者
以矧夫子爵不應謚而子孫又不稱字以别之
將謂之何哉若曰孔子則外之之辭而又孔
之通稱若曰夫子則又當時衆人相呼之通
不曰仲尼而何以哉嗟夫論語之於中庸同
理也夫子之於子思同一心也故曰中庸者孔
門傳授之心法也學者不求其言之異而求其
□之同則論語中庸皆可以一理貫之矣管見

translation_en:
… reason; with the Sage, he feared Zilu 子路 would lose the proper sequence of advancing in learning, whereas Zisi 子思 wished to hold up this classic to illuminate the far-reaching and subtle nature of the Way. How do the aims of the two books contradict each other?

When the Analects (Lunyu) says that "Song is insufficient to provide attestations," it laments the insufficiency of the documents and worthy men of Yin; when it says "I follow the men of former times," it speaks hypothetically: if one were to employ rites and music, one ought to pare away excess so as to attain the mean. Meanwhile, the Doctrine of the Mean (Zhongyong) speaks primarily from the standpoint of "being in a lower position and not rebelling": although the rites of Yin still survived, they were not the laws of the current age, and since Confucius (Kongzi 孔子) did not attain a ruling position, he simply followed the institutions of the reigning king.

When the Analects praises the "supreme virtue" of Zhou, it refers to King Wen 文王. Yet in the campaign to overthrow Zhou 紂, King Wen had the power to take the realm and did not take it, whereas King Wu 武王 had no personal desire to take it and yet could not avoid taking it; both simply obeyed Heaven in everything. Since they obeyed Heaven in everything, this did no harm to carrying on the intentions and continuing the undertakings of one's predecessors, which is why the Doctrine of the Mean praises him for it. How do the words of the two occasions [?] contradict each other?

Zisi was the Master's grandson, yet the Doctrine of the Mean directly calls him by his style name "Zhongni" 仲尼. This is because in antiquity, when someone held no noble rank in life and received no posthumous title at death, there were cases where descendants referred to them by their personal name. How much more so since the Master's rank did not entitle him to a posthumous title—if his descendants did not even use his style name to distinguish him, what were they to call him? To say "Kongzi" would be the language of an outsider, and moreover a general designation for the Kong clan; to say "Master" (Fuzi 夫子) would likewise be a general term by which everyone addressed one another at the time. If he did not call him "Zhongni," what else could he use?

Alas! The Analects and the Doctrine of the Mean share one and the same principle; the Master and Zisi shared one and the same mind. Thus it is said that the Doctrine of the Mean is the method of the mind transmitted within the Confucian school. If scholars do not seek out the differences in their words, but instead seek the sameness of their [intent/principle], then the Analects and the Doctrine of the Mean can both be threaded together by a single principle. My humble view…

所以作也當是之時見而知之者惟曾氏之傳
得其宗此傳之十章所由述也自是而後正學

translation_en:
…in books, the essentials of the Great Way are handed down as a standard for later generations. Understanding this, one can then reply to Your Excellency's enlightened question.

In antiquity, the method of teaching people how to pursue learning went no further than the Great Learning (Daxue). For the book of the Great Learning takes the investigation of things, the extension of knowledge, making the intentions sincere, and rectifying the mind as the means of cultivating oneself; and it takes regulating the family, rightly governing the state, and bringing peace to all under Heaven as the Way of governing others. If one studies without following this, one will be confined to the trivialities of rote recitation and literary composition, which is not what is called orthodox learning. If one governs without basing oneself on this, one will degenerate into the errors of harsh punishments and legalism—how could that be called good governance?

From the times of Tang, Yu, and the Three Dynasties onward, those who achieved prominence above and bore the responsibilities of ruler and teacher have been many, yet in personally practicing this Way to govern, they differed. Such rulers as Yao, Shun, and Yu, who sincerely held fast the Mean, and Tang and Wu, who established the Mean and established the Supreme Standard, were all purely in accord with the Way of the Great Learning. Tai Jia, who was able to bring his virtue to completion, and Kings Cheng and Kang, who followed the great laws, came close to the Way of the Great Learning. As for the tyranny of Jie and Zhou, the waylessness of Kings You and Li, and Emperors Yuan and Cheng of the Han—did they not act contrary to this Way? This is why Your Excellency sighs that those above could not all practice its Way.

Those who remained in obscurity below as sages and worthies have also been many, yet in elucidating this Way to show it to others, they likewise differed. Our Master [Confucius], possessing virtue but no official position, took the methods of the former kings, recited them, and transmitted them to instruct later generations; this is why the Classic text of the Great Learning was composed. At that time, among those who saw and understood it, only the transmission of Master Zeng (Zengzi) grasped its fundamental principle; this is why the ten chapters of Commentary were written. From that time onward, orthodox learning…

translation_en:
… was not transmitted. As for the Discourse on the Mean (Zhongshuo) of Master Wenzhong [Wang Tong] and the "Inquiry on the Way" (Yuan Dao) of Han Changli [Han Yu], were they not cases of roughly understanding how to manifest luminous virtue and renew the people, without seeking to abide in the highest good? As for others—such as the laws and ordinances of Guan Zhong, the punishments and names (xingming) of Shang Yang, and the followers of Shen Buhai and Han Fei—were they not cases of failing to strive to manifest their own luminous virtue, while merely regarding administrative orders and legal regulations as sufficient to renew the people? This is why Your Excellency sighs that those below cannot all elucidate this Way.

Now, to elucidate it is surely to wish to put it into practice. The various Confucians of the Song dynasty were not unversed in orthodox learning. For instance, the Masters Cheng of Henan [Cheng Hao and Cheng Yi] once singled out and honored this book from within the Record of Ritual by Dai (Daiji), arranging the order of its bamboo slips and bringing out its ultimate meaning, so that its Way shone brightly and was once again made clear to the world. Thereafter, Master Zhu of Ziyang [Zhu Xi] also compiled and edited this book and presented lectures on it before Emperor Ningzong, speaking at every turn of making the intentions sincere; thus this Way was almost on the verge of being put into practice! Why was it, then, that not long after lecturing at court he was abruptly reassigned to a provincial post? This is why the governance of the Song stopped at being merely that of the Song, and in the end could not match antiquity.

At present, the Sacred Son of Heaven reigns above, daily attending the Classics Mat (jingyan) to lecture on and elucidate the Great Learning (Daxue). Not only does he grasp it in his mind, he also embodies it in his person; thus, his extension of orthodox learning to bring about good governance can rival the glory of Tang [Yao], Yu [Shun], and the Three Dynasties. How fortunate indeed are this age and this people!

For if instruction and nourishment lack a method, the people's livelihood will not be fulfilled and ritual propriety and righteousness will have no means to arise; if encouragement and chastisement lack a system, the worthy and the unworthy will be confounded and transformative governance will have no means to flourish. translation_en: …one must regulate their fields and homesteads and teach them arboriculture and animal husbandry, so as to fulfill the way of nourishing them; and one must attend carefully to the instruction of the local schools and reiterate the principles of filial piety and fraternal respect, so as to fulfill the way of educating them. If these two undertakings are not entrusted to the right men, how could this be achieved? When officials are unequal to their duties, the people have no peace; therefore officials cannot be without encouragement and chastisement. If one wishes to make officials equal to their duties, possessing the ethos of upright and benevolent administrators and free of greedy and corrupt conduct, then one must make their selection and appointment impartial, so that the worthy may all advance to receive noble ranks and rewards; and one must make their merit evaluations strict, so that the unworthy cannot by luck escape punishments and penalties. If these two measures are not carried out according to the proper way, how could one attain this? Moreover, to speak of education and nourishment: nowadays corvée is lightened and taxes are reduced, the agricultural seasons are not violated, and farming and sericulture are by no means neglected; stipends are generous, labor services are remitted, Confucian teachers are carefully chosen, and schools are by no means left in disrepair. Yet although farming and sericulture are promoted, the people's resources for food and clothing are sometimes still insufficient; this is because those in charge of farming and sericulture merely pursue the name without the diligence of leading in person. And although schools are maintained, the custom of ritual deference among the people has still not arisen; this is because those in charge of schools merely attend to superficialities without the substance of personal practice. If indeed those in charge of farming and sericulture were all like Huang Ba 黃霸 in Yingchuan 潁川, encouraging the people to plow and sow, and those who promote schools were all like Wen Weng 文翁 when governing Shu Commandery 蜀郡, transforming students through instruction, what worry would there still be that the people would not have every household provided for and every person well-off, or that customs and mores would not be transformed? 同考試官贊善錢　批　馬政雖一事而能詳
究無遺措置有術使推而達諸用亦何
施而不可耶文云乎哉
考試官洗馬李　批　此卷前二場已在優選
策場數問皆有快人意處宜後此
punctuated:
徇一己之私；刑罰雖嚴，而貪墨之風猶自若也，以典廉察之任者，或未能合天下之公。誠使職銓選者，皆如唐虞之九載三考而黜陟其幽明；司考覈者，皆如成周以六計弊吏而大行夫誅賞，尚何患乎吏不守法奉公而循良愷悌歟？夫有宜於古，必有宜於今。古人所以致治者，用此道也；今豈有行之而不效乎？特奉行者之未至耳。孔子曰：「為政在人。」又曰：「其人存則其政舉。」鯫生學不足以博古，才不足以通今，其於經世之術，茫乎未有聞焉。茲承明問，姑摭所聞以對，惟進教之，幸甚。

第五問
彭華
同考試官贊善錢批：馬政雖一事，而能詳究無遺，措置有術。使推而達諸用，亦何施而不可耶？文云乎哉！

translation_en:
…indulging their own personal partialities; and although punishments and penalties are strict, the trend of greed and corruption remains as before, because those in charge of investigatory supervision have perhaps failed to align with the impartiality of the realm. If those responsible for personnel selection were truly all as in the era of Tang and Yu, conducting three evaluations over nine years to demote the unenlightened and promote the enlightened; and if those in charge of performance scrutiny were all as in the era of the Complete Zhou, using the Six Criteria to judge officials and grandly carrying out punishments and rewards, then what worry would there still be that officials would not abide by the law, serve the public good, and be upright, virtuous, and benevolent? Now, what was suitable for antiquity must also be suitable for the present. That by which the ancients achieved good governance was the use of this very Way; how could it be practiced today and not prove effective? It is merely that those who implement it have not yet reached the mark. Confucius said: "Governance lies in men." He also said: "When the right men are present, that governance flourishes." As a lowly scholar, my learning is insufficient to encompass antiquity, and my talent is insufficient to comprehend the present; as for the art of ordering the world, I am at a loss and have heard nothing of it. Now, having received your enlightened question, I merely gather what I have heard in order to reply, and only beg that you advance and instruct me—that would be the greatest fortune.

心於所學者歟春闈首選輿論固

translation_en:
…essay gives an even more detailed point-by-point response regarding the institutional system of horse administration. Surely he is one who has truly applied his mind to what he has studied! Public opinion certainly assigns to him first place in the Metropolitan Examination.

Examiner and Chancellor Shang [Shang Lu 商輅] comments: The policy essays all answer the questions well, and the one on horse administration is especially detailed. His statement that the method of raising horses lies in securing the right land and the right men is truly a sound argument. Excelling in all three sessions, he deserves first place.

To discuss the methods of horse administration, one must examine antiquity and adapt to the present; to elaborate on the efficacy of horse administration, it lies in securing the right land and employing the right men. For if one examines antiquity without adapting to the present, one certainly cannot exhaustively realize its methods; and if one secures the right land without employing the right men, how could that suffice to achieve its efficacy? Ever since the Six Ministers of the Institutions of Zhou (Zhou dian), the Minister of War (Zhengguan) was called the Marshal (Sima), because horses are what governance values most and what military forces rely upon to achieve victory. At that time, the Corral Officers (Jiaoren) were in charge of the administration of the king's horses, distinguishing the sechs categories of horses: there were what were called stud horses (zhongma), road horses (daoma), and war horses (rongma), and there were what were called hunting horses (tianma), ceremonial horses (qima), and common work horses (numa)—thus the breeds of horses were distinct. Whenever fine horses were distributed to be reared in teams of four (sheng), each team of four horses had one master (shi) and four grooms (yu); three teams of four made a stall (zao), and each stall had one Equerry (Quma); three stalls made a tether-group (xi), and each tether-group had one Charioteer (Yufu); six tether-groups made a stable (jiu), and each stable had one Chief Groom (Pufu); six stables formed a corral (jiao), and the corrals had left and right divisions. Thus the administration of rearing horses had its gradations, and those in charge of them each had their respective subordinates. Whether in the suburbs of the Son of Heaven, the states of the feudal lords, or the households of the grandees and servicemen, there were none that did not have horses; and as for the districts of sixty-four well-fields (qiudian) annually supplying four horses,…

秦開阡陌廢田賦由是馬政日弛而外患遂生

人至於邊郡之盛則三十六苑分置西北及武
帝有事征伐而馬課遂及於四方矣此漢之馬
政大抵牧於民而用於官也唐府兵之制當給
馬者官與其直不任戰者鬻之以錢不足則府
供之蓋唐承天下征伐之弊馬耗殆盡麟德之
間始得張萬歲為太僕而馬至七十萬餘分四
===
十八監各置所以領之天寶之後馬復耗損
及王毛仲為使又與麟德相等矣此唐之馬政
大抵牧於官而用於民也迨至有宋始養之於
官曰官馬後畜之於民曰戸馬又其後市於戎
狄曰戎馬其市戎馬之制始易以銅鐵戎因獲
其器次易以銀絹戎復獲其用當時議者謂莫
若易之以茶則在我足以為利在彼不足以為

punctuated: 則牧於民者。此成周官民通牧之制，可謂善矣。秦開阡陌，廢田賦，由是馬政日弛，而外患遂生。漢初稍復古制，勸民養馬，有一匹者，復卒三人。至於邊郡之盛，則三十六苑分置西北；及武帝有事征伐，而馬課遂及於四方矣。此漢之馬政，大抵牧於民而用於官也。唐府兵之制，當給馬者，官與其直；不任戰者，鬻之以錢，不足則府供之。蓋唐承天下征伐之弊，馬耗殆盡，麟德之間，始得張萬歲為太僕，而馬至七十萬餘，分四十八監，各置所以領之；天寶之後，馬復耗損，及王毛仲為使，又與麟德相等矣。此唐之馬政，大抵牧於官而用於民也。迨至有宋，始養之於官，曰官馬；後畜之於民，曰戸馬；又其後市於戎狄，曰戎馬。其市戎馬之制，始易以銅鐵，戎因獲其器；次易以銀絹，戎復獲其用。當時議者謂莫若易之以茶，則在我足以為利，在彼不足以為我害，庶為計之得耳。此歷代之馬政然也。方今監寺有馬，郡邑有馬，是即成周官民通牧之意……
translation_en:
…were pastured among the people. This system of the flourishing Zhou, in which both the state and the people jointly pastured horses, may indeed be called admirable.

When the Qin opened up the grid of footpaths between fields and abolished the land-unit military levy, horse administration grew daily more lax, and foreign threats consequently arose. At the beginning of the Han, the ancient system was gradually restored: the people were encouraged to raise horses, and anyone who had one horse was exempted from three conscript laborers' service. At the height of prosperity in the frontier commanderies, thirty-six pasturages were distributed across the northwest; when Emperor Wu undertook military campaigns, horse quotas extended throughout the four quarters of the realm. Thus the horse administration of the Han, in general, had horses pastured by the people and used by the state.

Under the garrison militia (fubing) system of the Tang, for those who were to be supplied with horses, the government provided their price; horses unfit for battle were sold for cash, and if the proceeds fell short, the garrison made up the difference. Because the Tang inherited the exhaustion of empire-wide warfare, its horses had been nearly depleted. During the Linde era (664–665), it first obtained Zhang Wansui 張萬歲 as Chief Minister of the Court of the Imperial Stud (Taipu), and the horses reached more than 700,000, divided among forty-eight directorates (jian), each establishing an office to superintend them. After the Tianbao era (742–756) [?], the horses again suffered depletion, yet when Wang Maozhong 王毛仲 served as commissioner, their numbers once more equaled those of the Linde era. Thus the horse administration of the Tang, in general, had horses pastured by the state and used by the people.

Down to the Song dynasty, at first horses were raised by the government and called "government horses" (guanma); later they were kept by the people and called "household horses" (huma); and still later they were purchased from the western and northern tribes and called "tribal horses" (rongma). Under the system for purchasing tribal horses, at first they were traded for copper and iron, whereby the tribesmen acquired weapons; next they were traded for silver and silk, whereby the tribesmen again acquired useful wealth. Commentators at the time maintained that nothing was better than trading tea for them: on our side it sufficed to yield profit, while on their side it could not be used to do us harm, which was perhaps the most advantageous plan. Such was the horse administration of successive dynasties.

At present, the directorates and courts have horses, and the prefectures and counties have horses; this is none other than the flourishing Zhou's principle of joint pasturing by the state and the people…

translation_en: … [spirit]. Yet for those pastured by the state, the people supply the fodder and grain; and for those pastured by the people, the officials demand breeding quotas and compensation for losses, so that by this means the people are sometimes burdened. Alas! Rather than pasturing them among the people, it is better to pasture them under the state; and rather than pasturing them under the state, it is still better to pasture them in spacious and open lands. For the breeding and multiplication of horses depend upon the land, while the increase or decrease of their numbers depends upon the men in charge. When we observe that the Han had thirty-six pasturages (yuan) and the Tang had forty-eight directorates of horse pasturage (jian), we see that the land cannot but be carefully chosen. And when we observe that the Tang obtained a single Zhang Wansui 張萬歲 and the number of horses doubled, and later obtained a single Wang Maozhong 王毛仲 and the number of horses did not dwindle, we see that the men cannot but be carefully chosen. As a plan for the present, nothing is better than to select fine pastures and supply them with mares. For those in the prefectures and counties, responsibility should be placed upon the prefects and magistrates; for those along the frontiers, responsibility should be placed upon the generals and commanders. If we do not press them for immediate results, but grant them ample time over the months and years, we shall see after several years that horses will form great herds in the frontier prefectures and their numbers will multiply abundantly. What worry would there be that our troops are not strong or that invaders and enemies are not repelled! Foolish as I am, I have clung narrowly to a single classic and have not yet thoroughly investigated horse administration. Now, having received your enlightened question, I respectfully set forth this broad outline in reply, begging only that you admit me and instruct me further.

translation_en:
Postface to the Record of the Metropolitan Examination

Heaven has favored the August Ming with possession of All under Heaven, and the successive sagely emperors, succeeding one another and obeying Heaven to plan for governance, have likewise established the civil service examinations to select scholars as their assistants. His Majesty, having inherited the Great Succession and ably furthered the illustrious achievements of his predecessors, has given even greater weight and care to the institution of promoting the worthy. In the spring of the fifth year of the Jingtai reign (1454), the year of the triennial examination, scholars from across the empire who came to sit for the examination numbered over three thousand. Following precedent, the Ministry of Rites submitted a memorial requesting examiners, and His Majesty appointed your servants [Shang] Lu 商輅 and [Li] Shao 李紹, while instructing the relevant authorities to prohibit fraud and malfeasance, maintain strict precautions, and enforce severe penalties for favoritism. translation_en: … this command, we have been reverent and fearful day and night. In grading and comparing the papers, we eliminated nine out of ten, striving to maintain the utmost impartiality so as to fulfill His Majesty's intentions. Once the thorny barriers of the examination compound were removed, the three hundred and fifty men selected were all those whose essays conformed to the standards and were worthy of note. Oh, how magnificent! Your servant venture to think that in selecting scholars, the dynasty places particular weight on the category of metropolitan graduates (jinshi); scholars who are outstanding and extraordinary, who study diligently and master the Classics, indeed all advance by this path. Yet they must first have their names inscribed on the rolls in the provinces before they can be examined at the Ministry of Rites; and they must also have their names inscribed at the Ministry of Rites before they can reply to the Emperor's questions in the Great Court. Once they have replied in the Great Court, they are thereupon granted offices and given salaries. Their selection is strict, their treatment is generous, and their employment is not undertaken lightly. translation_en: …this; truly it is a grand institution rare in the world! Meeting with this auspicious era of sacred enlightenment, you scholars have been able to take part in this selection, and will soon respond in the great court, thereby enjoying noble rank and ascending to illustrious prominence. How could you not reflect on how to repay and prove worthy of this! For attending to affairs with diligence, regulating oneself with integrity, benefiting the people with benevolence, and serving the sovereign with loyalty—these several principles are the great fundamentals of official service. From this day forward, may you scholars strive to keep these in your hearts and uphold them in your conduct: do not be encumbered by selfish interests, do not bow to power, do not grow arrogant because of your position, and do not become extravagant because of your emolument. translation_en:
…the state and the people is truly rooted in this; and in future days, glorious honor and illustrious greatness will also begin from here. May all of you scholars mutually strive toward this.
